recall_basic.q: Who is the only person who can legally obligate the Government on a contract?
recall_basic.a: The contracting officer (CO), through a warrant.

recall_basic.q: Your real value as a 1102 isn't running the package — it's what?
recall_basic.a: Business judgment — sound, defensible decisions.

recall_basic.topic: The Players: Roles & Who Does What
recall_basic.q: Can a COR change a contract's price, scope, or terms?
recall_basic.a: No — only the CO can.

recall_basic.topic: The Players: Roles & Who Does What
recall_basic.q: Who certifies that funds are available?
recall_basic.a: Financial Management (FM / Comptroller).

recall_basic.q: What document makes someone a CO?
recall_basic.a: A written warrant (SF 1402).

recall_basic.q: Someone without authority tells a contractor to start work — what is that, and is the Government bound?
recall_basic.a: An unauthorized commitment (UAC); not bound unless it's ratified.

recall_basic.topic: The Rulebook: The RFO, R-DFARS & DAF Policy
recall_basic.q: What's the governing rulebook now, and what's being retired?
recall_basic.a: The RFO and R-DFARS; the legacy FAR / DFARS / DAFFARS.

recall_basic.topic: The Rulebook: The RFO, R-DFARS & DAF Policy
recall_basic.q: Where do you confirm a current threshold or rule?
recall_basic.a: acquisition.gov/far-overhaul — never quote from memory.

recall_basic.topic: Colors of Money & Fiscal Law Basics
recall_basic.q: Name the three-part fiscal test.
recall_basic.a: Time · Purpose · Amount (TPA).

recall_basic.topic: Colors of Money & Fiscal Law Basics
recall_basic.q: Can you use this year's money for next year's need?
recall_basic.a: Generally no — the bona fide need rule.

recall_basic.q: What runs underneath every phase of the lifecycle?
recall_basic.a: The contract file / documentation (and oversight).

recall_basic.q: If it isn't in the file…
recall_basic.a: …it didn't happen. The file tells the story of every decision.

recall_basic.q: What does market research tell you?
recall_basic.a: Who can perform, whether it's commercial, whether small businesses can compete, and a realistic price.

recall_basic.q: What's the Government's own price estimate called?
recall_basic.a: The IGCE (Independent Government Cost Estimate).

recall_basic.q: What's the default for buys over the SAT ($350K)?
recall_basic.a: Full and open competition.

recall_basic.q: If you can't compete it, what do you need?
recall_basic.a: A justification (J&A) under a recognized exception.

recall_basic.q: Micro-purchase threshold?
Simplified Acquisition Threshold (SAT)?
On a firm-fixed-price contract, who bears the cost risk?
recall_basic.a: The contractor.

recall_basic.q: When is a cost-type contract appropriate?
recall_basic.a: When the work is too uncertain to price firmly (e.g., R&D).

recall_basic.q: What's the goal of price analysis, and is it always required?
recall_basic.a: A fair and reasonable price — and yes, always.

recall_basic.q: Mod adds $1M and deletes $1M — what value counts for the certified-data threshold?
recall_basic.a: $2M (absolute value of each, not the net).

recall_basic.q: Section L vs. Section M?
recall_basic.a: L = how to submit; M = how you'll be evaluated.

recall_basic.q: What is "best value"?
recall_basic.a: The best mix of price and non-price factors for the Government.

recall_basic.q: What are you protecting during a source selection?
recall_basic.a: Source-selection information and contractor proposal data (the PIA).

recall_basic.q: You spot an integrity problem — first move?
recall_basic.a: Stop, and call your CO and JA (legal) immediately.

recall_basic.q: State the Rule of Two.
recall_basic.a: Set it aside if you expect two or more small businesses to compete at fair market prices.

recall_basic.q: What drives the small-business size standard?
recall_basic.a: The NAICS code you assign.

recall_basic.topic: Contract Administration: Mods, Options, Claims & Terminations
recall_basic.q: Who watches contractor performance day-to-day?
recall_basic.a: The COR — but only the CO changes the deal.

recall_basic.topic: Contract Administration: Mods, Options, Claims & Terminations
recall_basic.q: A change so big it goes beyond the original contract's scope is a…?
recall_basic.a: Cardinal change — it needs new competition or a J&A, not a modification.

recall_advanced.q: Five factors in the competitive-vs-sole-source call.
recall_advanced.a: Data rights sufficiency · switching/qualification costs · industrial base capability · honest urgency · second-source economics.

recall_advanced.q: What inventory precedes a sustainment competition decision?
recall_advanced.a: Data rights, deliverables (source/build/interfaces), GFP/tooling, licenses, funding.

recall_advanced.q: What can never justify a bridge?
recall_advanced.a: Lack of advance planning.

recall_advanced.q: What factors drive competitive vs. sole-source for the follow-on?
recall_advanced.a: Data rights and technical data sufficiency · qualification/switching costs and time · industrial base capability · urgency honestly assessed · lifecycle economics of a second source. Facts on each, in the file.

recall_advanced.q: How do you find out if other sources can perform?
recall_advanced.a: Fresh sources-sought and RFIs · industry days · capability analysis against the tech data package · other services'/agencies' experience with similar builds.

recall_advanced.q: And if truly no one else can?
recall_advanced.a: RFO 6.103-1, one responsible source — with the J&A at the right approval tier and market research that would survive a competitor's lawyer reading it.

recall_advanced.q: Three types of authority — which one binds nothing?
recall_advanced.a: Express, implied, apparent — apparent binds nothing.

recall_advanced.q: All six ratification elements.
recall_advanced.a: Proper-if-CO · benefit · ratifier's actual authority · fair & reasonable price · funds then and now · Legal.

recall_advanced.q: Who ratifies a $500K unauthorized commitment? A $90K one?
recall_advanced.a: $500K → HCA (delegable); $90K → COCO.

recall_advanced.q: Five elements of a valid contract.
recall_advanced.a: Offer/acceptance · consideration · competency · legality · certainty of terms.

recall_advanced.q: What if the Government received no benefit?
recall_advanced.a: Then it can't be ratified — a ratification requires acceptance or benefit. The contractor's remedy shifts to a claim (or quantum meruit through Legal); my job is the documented record either way.

recall_advanced.q: The person who did it refuses to write a statement.
recall_advanced.a: Document the refusal, reconstruct the facts from correspondence and witnesses, and proceed — the package needs the story, and the refusal itself goes in the record.

recall_advanced.q: Is implied authority real authority?
recall_advanced.a: Yes — authority reasonably inferred from a position's duties is legally valid. Apparent authority is the trap: looking authorized isn't being authorized.

recall_advanced.q: Two categories of protected information under RFO 3.104.
recall_advanced.a: Source selection information; contractor bid/proposal data.

recall_advanced.q: Your first two containment actions on a bad disclosure.
recall_advanced.a: Legal immediately; identify/contain — recipient deletes with signed confirmation.

recall_advanced.q: Where does the decision go if the disclosure impacts the procurement?
recall_advanced.a: The HCA.

recall_advanced.q: Name three prevention practices you'd brief a new source selection team.
recall_advanced.a: Two-person review before release · encryption with separate passwords · disable auto-complete · SSI cover sheets (any three).

recall_advanced.q: The recipient says she deleted it — done?
recall_advanced.a: Not on her word: signed affidavit confirming deletion of all copies, and the determination still has to be written. The record closes it, not the reply email.

recall_advanced.q: What if it went to an actual offeror?
recall_advanced.a: That's the high-impact branch: presumptive taint of the competition. HCA decision territory — disqualification or cancellation are on the table, with Legal driving.

recall_advanced.q: A contractor employee asks your evaluator how the ratings look — violation?
recall_advanced.a: Attempting to obtain source selection information is itself a PIA problem. Document it, report it, brief the team — silence is how small probes become disclosures.

recall_advanced.q: The three OCI types — and which is hardest to mitigate?
recall_advanced.a: Biased ground rules (hardest) · unequal access · impaired objectivity.

recall_advanced.q: The three handling tools, in order of preference.
recall_advanced.a: Avoid · neutralize · mitigate.

recall_advanced.q: Who approves an OCI waiver, and is it delegable?
recall_advanced.a: HCA; non-delegable.

recall_advanced.q: True or false: unequal access requires showing the contractor acted on the information.
recall_advanced.a: False — the access imbalance itself is the conflict.

recall_advanced.q: Which type is hardest to mitigate and why?
recall_advanced.a: Biased ground rules — once the requirement itself is shaped, a firewall can't un-shape it. Exclusion is the usual outcome.

recall_advanced.q: The contractor firewall says the proposal team never saw anything. Enough?
recall_advanced.a: A firewall can address unequal access going forward — it does nothing for ground rules already written. Type drives remedy.

recall_advanced.q: Who has final say on the mitigation plan?
recall_advanced.a: The PCO. Panels and reviewers advise; the decision and the accountability are mine.

recall_advanced.q: Recite the seven responsibility standards.
recall_advanced.a: Finances · schedule · performance · integrity · organization/experience/controls · equipment/facilities · qualified & eligible.

recall_advanced.q: Which two system checks precede award, and at what threshold does the second apply?
recall_advanced.a: SAM exclusions always; FAPIIS over SAT ($350K).

recall_advanced.q: What happens when a small business is found non-responsible?
recall_advanced.a: Referral to SBA — a CoC conclusively establishes responsibility.

recall_advanced.q: Doubt about capability cuts in whose favor?
recall_advanced.a: The Government's — doubt means no.

recall_advanced.q: SBA issues the CoC but you still think they'll fail. Now what?
recall_advanced.a: A CoC is conclusive as to responsibility — I award, then protect the Government with administration: a solid QASP, milestone surveillance, and early engagement at the first sign of trouble. (Appeal paths exist in a dollar band — worked with Legal and SBA, not solo.)

recall_advanced.q: Can you use responsibility to screen out a contractor you distrust?
recall_advanced.a: Only on the standards, only on facts. Distrust without documentation is how a defensible "no" becomes a sustained protest.

recall_advanced.q: What's the difference between non-responsible and ineligible?
recall_advanced.a: Ineligible = excluded (SAM/debarment) — no award, period. Non-responsible = fails the standards for this award, on today's facts.

recall_advanced.q: Four questions market research must answer.
recall_advanced.a: Capable sources · commercial or not · small business capability · industry practices (also: bundling justified?).

recall_advanced.q: How long is research treated as current?
recall_advanced.a: 18 months.

recall_advanced.q: Name five research methods.
recall_advanced.a: Sources sought · RFI · industry day · SME/vendor engagement · prior-buy history · catalogs (any five).

recall_advanced.q: What document downstream decisions cite — and what happens if it was never written?
recall_advanced.a: The market research report; undocumented research can't support the J&A/set-aside/CID that relies on it.

recall_advanced.q: Your sources-sought got one response. Sole source it?
recall_advanced.a: One response to one notice isn't market absence — it's a data point. Widen the net (direct outreach, industry channels, adjacent NAICS) before concluding only one source exists; the J&A will be judged on the effort.

recall_advanced.q: How is market research different from a competition requirement?
recall_advanced.a: Research is the evidence; competition is the decision. Research tells me whether the Rule of Two is met, whether full-and-open is realistic, whether commercial procedures fit — it doesn't replace any of them.

recall_advanced.q: The PM wrote the spec around Vendor X's product. Fix it with research?
recall_advanced.a: Backwards — research should shape the requirement, not justify it after the fact. I'd push for a performance-based restatement and use the research to show what the market can actually deliver.

recall_advanced.q: The supplies priority order, top to bottom.
recall_advanced.a: Inventory → excess → UNICOR → AbilityOne → wholesale → mandatory FSS → commercial.

recall_advanced.q: What leads the services ladder?
recall_advanced.a: AbilityOne.

recall_advanced.q: On an FSS order, who determines the order price fair and reasonable?
recall_advanced.a: The ordering contracting officer — GSA's schedule pricing doesn't substitute.

recall_advanced.q: The AbilityOne item is pricier than the commercial one. Buy commercial?
recall_advanced.a: Mandatory means mandatory — if the item is on the procurement list and meets the need, price alone doesn't unlock the open market. Work fit/availability issues through the program, on the record.

recall_advanced.q: Why isn't a schedule buy automatically fair and reasonable?
recall_advanced.a: Because GSA negotiated a ceiling across the government, not my quantity, configuration, or competitive moment. Comparing quotes among holders and asking for discounts is the ordering CO's job.

recall_advanced.q: The commercial definition in one sentence, including the mod rule.
recall_advanced.a: Sold/leased/licensed to the general public (or evolved and available in time), including minor mods that don't alter form, fit, or function.

recall_advanced.q: CID: at what threshold is it written, and who approves it?
recall_advanced.a: Over SAT ($350K); one level above the CO.

recall_advanced.q: Streamlined commercial procedures — cite and ceiling?
Name two things Part 12 gives you and two things it takes away.
recall_advanced.a: Gets: no certified data, streamlined terms/FFP preference. Takes: only customary market data rights; Part 49 termination machinery.

recall_advanced.q: How do you price it fair and reasonable without cost data?
recall_advanced.a: Market evidence: competition first, then catalog/published prices, sales history to other customers, parametric comparisons — and I can require data other than certified where the market evidence is thin.

recall_advanced.q: The mod adds an encrypted military datalink. Still minor?
recall_advanced.a: Test it against form, fit, and function of the base item — a modification that changes what the item fundamentally is or does takes you out of "minor." That's a facts-and-engineering call, documented in the CID.

recall_advanced.q: Termination for cause vs. T4D?
recall_advanced.a: Commercial contracts use the commercial clause's cause/convenience framework — Part 49's default machinery (cure notices per 49.x, excess reprocurement) doesn't apply as such. Chain warning: boards love this seam.

recall_advanced.q: The three SAP lanes and their dollar boundaries.
recall_advanced.a: GPC ≤$15K · POs $15K–$350K · BPAs for repetitive needs.

recall_advanced.q: Who is the MPT-to-SAT band reserved for?
recall_advanced.a: Small business, unless capable small sources can't be found.

recall_advanced.q: What documentation does an under-SAT sole source need?
recall_advanced.a: A documented single-source rationale + price reasonableness — no formal J&A.

recall_advanced.q: Commercial streamlined ceiling and cite?
Why not spread the tool-crib buy across three GPC swipes?
recall_advanced.a: That's splitting a known requirement to evade the MPT — a bright-line violation. One $210K requirement is one purchase-order action with small business first.

recall_advanced.q: BPA vs. IDIQ — when does the small path stop fitting?
recall_advanced.a: A BPA is an account, not a contract — no obligation until a call. When needs get big, defined, and multi-year, the structure (and the money) belongs in a real vehicle.

recall_advanced.q: One quote came back on your $80K buy — award?
recall_advanced.a: I can, if I can call the price fair and reasonable — compare to history, catalogs, IGCE, and document it. Reasonableness rides on evidence, not on the count of quotes.

recall_advanced.q: State the Rule of Two precisely.
recall_advanced.a: Reasonable expectation of two or more capable small businesses submitting offers at fair market prices → set aside.

recall_advanced.q: Sole-source ceilings: HUBZone other? SDVOSB other? 8(a) DoD?
What form documents specialist coordination?
recall_advanced.a: DD Form 2579.

recall_advanced.q: Subcontracting plan thresholds?
recall_advanced.a: $900K; $2M construction.

recall_advanced.q: Only one small business responds to your set-aside — now what?
recall_advanced.a: If the offer is fair-market priced, award — the Rule of Two tests the expectation, not the final count. Document what changed between research and offers.

recall_advanced.q: The requirement's been in the 8(a) program — can you compete it full-and-open now?
recall_advanced.a: Not unilaterally: once in 8(a), it stays unless SBA agrees to release it. That's the follow-on trap on 8(a) requirements.

recall_advanced.q: When does 8(a) sole source need a J&A?
recall_advanced.a: DoD: not below $100M. The program's statutory basis covers it — that's the 'authorized by statute' lane.

recall_advanced.q: Recite the four SAMO carve-outs.
recall_advanced.a: SAP · statute · in-scope mods · orders under existing vehicles.

recall_advanced.q: Name all seven RFO 6.103 exceptions, in any order.
recall_advanced.a: One source · urgency · industrial mobilization/R&D · international agreement · statute · national security · public interest.

recall_advanced.q: Your J&A is $18M — who approves? $95M (DoD)? $160M (DoD)?
recall_advanced.a: $18M → Competition Advocate; $95M DoD → HPA/PEO (DoD line is $150M); $160M DoD → SPE.

recall_advanced.q: How long do you have to post a J&A to SAM.gov after award? After an urgency award?
recall_advanced.a: 14 days; 30 days for urgency.

recall_advanced.q: Only one offer came in on your competitive solicitation — now what?
recall_advanced.a: If the solicitation allowed under 30 days for offers, consult the requiring activity and resolicit for at least 30. If interest was real but only one firm bid, find out why — get feedback, document it, and use it to open the next competition. The award can still be made if the price is fair and reasonable.

recall_advanced.q: What's the difference between full-and-open after exclusion of sources and other than full-and-open?
recall_advanced.a: Exclusion still competes — among a deliberately narrowed field (a set-aside is the everyday example). "Other than" means one or very few sources under an RFO 6.103 exception.

recall_advanced.q: Who approves your $40M J&A? …and a $15M one?
recall_advanced.a: $40M → HPA/PEO. $15M → Competition Advocate. (Know your ladder cold — boards love the second ask.)

recall_advanced.q: The program wants a bridge while the follow-on catches up. Fine?
recall_advanced.a: Only for a genuinely unforeseen cause — a protest, a directed strategy change, a regulatory change. "We didn't plan" is never a valid basis, and repeat bridges escalate to higher approval each time.

recall_advanced.q: The three exchange types and the line between them.
recall_advanced.a: Clarifications (minor, no revisions) · communications (pre-range) · discussions (post-range, meaningful, all in range).

recall_advanced.q: Who evaluates, who decides, who runs the business side?
recall_advanced.a: SSEB · SSA · PCO.

recall_advanced.q: When can you award without discussions?
recall_advanced.a: Solicitation said so and initial proposals support it.

recall_advanced.q: What must a post-award debrief include — and exclude?
recall_advanced.a: Include: evaluated result, significant weaknesses, ranking/rationale. Exclude: other offerors' proposal contents.

recall_advanced.q: Award without discussions — when is that OK?
recall_advanced.a: If the solicitation preserved it and the initial proposals support a clean award. On large, complex actions, discussions usually earn their keep — say you'd weigh it, not autopilot it.

recall_advanced.q: An evaluator wants to ping an offeror about an ambiguity before the range.
recall_advanced.a: That's a communication — through me, documented, no proposal revisions. The moment it invites a revision, it's discussions, and discussions have rules.

recall_advanced.q: Can price be a rating like technical?
recall_advanced.a: No — cost/price is evaluated (analysis, realism where applicable) but never adjectivally rated. It competes in the tradeoff as a number with analysis behind it.

recall_advanced.q: What makes discussions 'meaningful'?
recall_advanced.a: Each offeror hears its own significant weaknesses and deficiencies with enough substance to respond — tailored, not generic, and even-handed across the range.

recall_advanced.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
recall_advanced.q: Current certified-data threshold, and the date line that changed it?
recall_advanced.a: $10M for actions entered after 30 Jun 2026 (FY26 NDAA §1804); $2.5M for earlier contracts and their mods.

recall_advanced.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
recall_advanced.q: Recite CLAWM — and where do the exceptions live in the RFO?
recall_advanced.a: Commercial · Law/regulation · Adequate price competition · Waiver (HCA) · commercial Mods — RFO 15.403-2.

recall_advanced.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
recall_advanced.q: Which analysis is always required? When does cost realism apply?
recall_advanced.a: Price analysis, always (15.404-1); cost realism on competitive cost-type source selections (15.404-3).

recall_advanced.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
recall_advanced.q: All five elements of defective pricing.
recall_advanced.a: Was cost/pricing data · existed pre-agreement · not disclosed · relied upon · increased the price.

recall_advanced.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
recall_advanced.q: CPFF fee ceilings for R&D, most others, A&E.

recall_advanced.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
recall_advanced.q: What's the difference between certified and other-than-certified cost or pricing data?
recall_advanced.a: The data can be identical — the certificate is the difference. Other-than-certified is what you request to determine price reasonableness when an exception applies; no certificate, no defective-pricing remedy.

recall_advanced.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
recall_advanced.q: The contractor did a 'sweep' after agreement and found new data — now what?
recall_advanced.a: Sweeps are recommended, not required. Before award: incorporate — if the corrected price is lower, adjust down; if higher, the contractor generally eats it unless it's unreasonable, and you may reopen. After award: that's defective pricing — the Government is entitled to a price reduction plus interest; bring in Legal.

recall_advanced.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
recall_advanced.q: The contractor refuses to provide further support during fact-finding.
recall_advanced.a: Document exactly what was requested and refused, use DCMA/DCAA to press the field organization, elevate through the contractor's management — and remember I can't award without determining the price fair and reasonable. No data, no deal, and the file shows why.

recall_advanced.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
recall_advanced.q: When would you get DCAA vs. DCMA support?
recall_advanced.a: Field pricing support scales with dollars and type — DCMA forward-pricing rate support around $2.5M+ (fixed-price) / $10M+ (cost-type); DCAA audit at $10M+ (fixed-price) / $100M+ (cost-type). Below those, my pricing office and I work it.

recall_advanced.q: Five type-selection factors.
recall_advanced.a: Requirement definition · estimate confidence · technical risk · competition · accounting system · acquisition history (any five).

recall_advanced.q: The PTA formula.
recall_advanced.a: PTA = (Ceiling − Target Price) ÷ Gov share + Target Cost.

recall_advanced.q: Two gates every cost-type contract must clear.
recall_advanced.a: Adequate accounting system; D&F.

recall_advanced.q: E.O. 14402 justification thresholds — DoD and most agencies.
recall_advanced.a: DoD $100M; most agencies $10M.

recall_advanced.q: Walk me through the PTA.
recall_advanced.a: The point where the ceiling takes over: (ceiling price minus target price) divided by the Government's share, plus target cost. Past it, each cost dollar comes out of profit — the contractor is effectively on FFP from there to the ceiling.

recall_advanced.q: Why not FFP the development effort — doesn't it protect us?
recall_advanced.a: A contractor forced to price the unknowable pads the price or fails trying — both cost the Government more. FFP on high-uncertainty work is risk denial, not risk transfer.

recall_advanced.q: CPFF vs. CPIF in one sentence each?
recall_advanced.a: CPFF: fee fixed at award regardless of cost outcome — buys effort under uncertainty. CPIF: fee slides with cost performance inside a min/max — buys cost discipline when a credible target exists.

recall_advanced.q: All six fair-opportunity exceptions.
recall_advanced.a: Urgency · only-one-capable · logical follow-on · minimum guarantee · statute · order-level small business set-aside.

recall_advanced.q: Order-debrief breakpoint? GAO order-protest thresholds?
recall_advanced.a: $7.5M; $35M DoD / $10M civilian (or scope/period/ceiling growth at any value).

recall_advanced.q: What document supports an over-SAT exception, and who approves at $12M?
recall_advanced.a: A D&A; $12M → Competition Advocate.

recall_advanced.q: What makes a follow-on 'logical' enough to use the exception?
recall_advanced.a: Genuine continuity economics — the original order was competed (or properly excepted), and switching performers mid-stream would cost duplication the Government can't recover. Used sparingly, documented hard, and it weakens every time you stack it.

recall_advanced.q: A holder complains the last three orders all went to one firm.
recall_advanced.a: They get the ombudsman, and I get a look in the mirror: consideration has to be real — rotating "considered but lost" paperwork isn't fair opportunity.

recall_advanced.q: Can you set aside an order for small business on a mixed vehicle?
recall_advanced.a: Yes — order-level set-asides are a recognized exception lane; document the Rule-of-Two logic among holders.

recall_advanced.q: The exercise gates, all of them.
recall_advanced.a: Funds · existing need · most advantageous (fresh market/price look) · not excluded in SAM · performance considered.

recall_advanced.q: What happens legally if the notice date passes?
recall_advanced.a: The unilateral right lapses — continuation is bilateral.

recall_advanced.q: The services duration rail and the extension-clause cap.
recall_advanced.a: ~5 years base+options; 6-month extension cap.

recall_advanced.q: Three situations where you shouldn't use options at all.
recall_advanced.a: No realistic exercise chance · volatile pricing · full requirement already known and funded.

recall_advanced.q: Market prices dropped 15% since award. Exercise anyway?
recall_advanced.a: Only if I can still call the option price the most advantageous path after an informal market check — otherwise the honest answer may be a new competition. The option price was reasonable then; the gate asks about now.

recall_advanced.q: You missed the notice window by a week.
recall_advanced.a: The unilateral right is gone. If continuing is still best, it's a bilateral agreement — negotiated, documented, and the contractor holds leverage. Then I fix the suspense system that let it slip.

recall_advanced.q: Performance is shaky — exercise and 'manage it'?
recall_advanced.a: The performance gate exists for exactly this. Options are leverage: a contractor renewed despite flags learns the flags don't matter. Decide with the record, not with inertia.

recall_advanced.q: Direct vs. assisted — the one-sentence difference and the document assisted requires.
recall_advanced.a: Direct: our CO orders on their vehicle; assisted: their shop buys for us — signed interagency agreement required.

recall_advanced.q: When does the Economy Act apply, and what paperwork rides with it?
recall_advanced.a: Only absent a more specific authority; MIPR + D&F (Government's interest, not better from private sector).

recall_advanced.q: Does sending funds to another agency stop the fiscal clock?
recall_advanced.a: No — purpose, time, and amount rules travel with the money.

recall_advanced.q: Why not just MIPR it and let them worry about it?
recall_advanced.a: Because accountability doesn't transfer with the money — the requirement, the fiscal rules, and the outcome are still ours. The D&F exists to prove we chose this lane deliberately.

recall_advanced.q: Direct vs. assisted — who's the contracting officer?
recall_advanced.a: Direct: our CO places the order under their contract's terms. Assisted: their CO acts for us under the interagency agreement — which is why that agreement must define roles before a dollar moves.

recall_advanced.q: When is the Economy Act the wrong cite?
recall_advanced.a: Whenever a more specific authority exists — schedules and GWACs carry their own authority. Citing the Economy Act for a schedule order tells the board you memorized a name, not a framework.

recall_advanced.q: TPA — say what each letter tests.
recall_advanced.a: Time = availability + bona fide need; Purpose = appropriated use; Amount = ADA limits.

recall_advanced.q: Colors and clocks: O&M, RDT&E, procurement.
recall_advanced.a: 1 · 2 · 3 years.

recall_advanced.q: Severable vs. non-severable funding rules.
recall_advanced.a: Severable ≤12 months, may cross FYs, current funds; non-severable fully funded up front.

recall_advanced.q: LoC vs. LoF — which contract, what notice?
recall_advanced.a: LoC on fully funded cost contracts, LoF on incremental — ~75% notice.

recall_advanced.q: The financing order of preference.
recall_advanced.a: Private → customary (PBP preferred) → unusual → advance payments.

recall_advanced.q: The contractor blew past the ceiling without notice and wants more money.
recall_advanced.a: The limitation clause allocates that risk: no timely notice, no entitlement to overrun funding — the Government may fund, but doesn't have to. Facts first: when did they know, when did they tell.

recall_advanced.q: Why are performance-based payments preferred over progress payments?
recall_advanced.a: They pay for demonstrated events, not incurred cost — better incentive alignment, recoverable in default, and less administration on costs.

recall_advanced.q: Can expired funds pay a claim on an old contract?
recall_advanced.a: Yes — within their 5-year expired window, for adjustments to obligations properly made when current. After cancellation, no.

recall_advanced.q: The three funding scenarios and the rights each produces.
recall_advanced.a: All Government $ → unlimited; mixed → GPR (converting to unlimited after the period); all private $ → limited (tech data)/restricted (software).

recall_advanced.q: Who bears the burden of proving a restriction?
recall_advanced.a: The contractor.

recall_advanced.q: What may the Government do with GPR data?
recall_advanced.a: Any Government purpose — including competitive reprocurement under protections; no commercial use.

recall_advanced.q: The challenge sequence, and what you must not do while it runs.
recall_advanced.a: Written challenge → contractor response (60 days) → CO final decision → appeal; honor the markings until resolved.

recall_advanced.q: Deliverables arrived unmarked. What rights do we have?
recall_advanced.a: Unmarked data delivered under the clause is effectively unrestricted in the Government's hands — but confirm through Legal before acting on it; the honest move is verifying, not pouncing.

recall_advanced.q: Can GPR data go to a competitor for the sustainment RFP?
recall_advanced.a: Yes — Government purposes include competitive reprocurement, with recipients under nondisclosure protections. That's exactly what GPR is for.

recall_advanced.q: The contractor says the whole system is proprietary because it 'integrates' their private-expense modules.
recall_advanced.a: Integration doesn't launder rights — map component by component. Mixed funding at the component level yields component-level rights, and the assertion list has to be that granular.

recall_advanced.q: The four scope-test corners.
recall_advanced.a: Competition anticipation · contract type · period · cumulative cost.

recall_advanced.q: Unilateral vs. bilateral — which actions belong to each?
recall_advanced.a: Unilateral: admin, in-scope change orders, option exercise; bilateral: substantive negotiated changes.

recall_advanced.q: Define constructive change and cardinal change in one sentence each.
recall_advanced.a: Constructive: Government conduct changes work without formal direction; cardinal: change so profound it exceeds what was competed — potential breach.

recall_advanced.q: Against what baseline is mod 100 judged?
recall_advanced.a: The original contract, all mods cumulative.

recall_advanced.q: Who decides if it's in scope?
recall_advanced.a: The PCO, with Legal — documented. It's a judgment call with a test, not a vibe: anticipation, type, period, cumulative cost.

recall_advanced.q: A competitor found out about a big unpublicized mod and complained. Your answer?
recall_advanced.a: If my scope analysis is in the file and honest, I walk them (and my boss) through it. If the analysis was never done — that's the finding. Publicity follows scope: in-scope mods aren't competed or synopsized; new work is.

recall_advanced.q: PM directed extra testing verbally; contractor performed. What is that?
recall_advanced.a: A constructive change candidate — Government conduct changed the work. Contractor asserts its costs; I sort entitlement and get the direction channel fixed (all direction through the PCO).

recall_advanced.q: The default rule and the four-part exception test.
recall_advanced.a: Contractor furnishes; GFP only if best interest · benefit > burden · no substantial risk increase · not otherwise met — all four.

recall_advanced.q: Who writes the GFP justification?
recall_advanced.a: The requiring activity (PM), to the PCO.

recall_advanced.q: Name three clause functions that ride with the property clause.
recall_advanced.a: Marking/IUID · loss reporting · property-system administration · disposal (any three).

recall_advanced.q: Consequence of delivering GFP late or faulty?
recall_advanced.a: Government-caused delay — schedule/equitable-adjustment exposure.

recall_advanced.q: Contractor reports a Government-furnished test set stolen.
recall_advanced.a: The loss-reporting clause machinery runs: report, investigate, determine liability under the risk allocation, and adjust the property record — with the property administrator carrying the process.

recall_advanced.q: Why not furnish property freely if it lowers proposed prices?
recall_advanced.a: Because price isn't the only ledger: administration, risk shift, and Government performance obligations all cost. The four-part test is that ledger.

recall_advanced.q: When is no justification needed?
recall_advanced.a: Property furnished for repair/modification/overhaul work — the property is the requirement there.

recall_advanced.q: The obligation caps, before and after the qualifying proposal.
recall_advanced.a: 50% of NTE before; 75% after.

recall_advanced.q: The definitization clock and its other trigger.
recall_advanced.a: 180 days from qualifying proposal; also when obligations reach the caps.

recall_advanced.q: Two reasons that never justify a UCA.
recall_advanced.a: Lack of planning; administrative convenience.

recall_advanced.q: UCO vs. UCA in one sentence.
recall_advanced.a: UCO = unpriced unilateral change within an existing contract's scope; UCA = new undefinitized contract action.

recall_advanced.q: The contractor is slow-rolling the qualifying proposal. Why might that be?
recall_advanced.a: Every month undefinitized is a month of cost-reimbursement-like comfort at negotiation leverage. My tools: the obligation caps bite, progress-payment posture tightens, and the definitization schedule is a contract term — enforce it.

recall_advanced.q: Why does fee usually come down at definitization?
recall_advanced.a: Weighted guidelines price risk. With actuals on the books, the cost risk the fee would have paid for has partly evaporated — fee follows the remaining risk, not the original unknowns.

recall_advanced.q: Do UCAs need clearance? A J&A?
recall_advanced.a: Clearance at definitization (award-stage clearance isn't the gate). And the circumstances driving a UCA usually drive a Part 6 exception too — urgency or one-source — so the J&A rides in parallel.

recall_advanced.q: Business vs. contract clearance — what each approves.
recall_advanced.a: Business = release the solicitation / open negotiations; contract = the award/negotiated result.

recall_advanced.q: Why must the reviewer be independent?
recall_advanced.a: The selector can't approve the selection — independent senior review before commitment.

recall_advanced.q: When does a UCA clear?
recall_advanced.a: At definitization.

recall_advanced.q: Why two clearances instead of one?
recall_advanced.a: Because a sound strategy can still yield a bad deal, and a good deal can implement an unapproved strategy — the gates catch different failures.

recall_advanced.q: What does the clearance authority actually check?
recall_advanced.a: That the action implements the approved strategy · the price/result is fair and reasonable and supported · the file complies — statute, regulation, policy — before the Government commits.

recall_advanced.q: Clearance said no. Now?
recall_advanced.a: Fix what they flagged — position, support, or strategy — and return. Clearance friction is cheaper than any failure it prevents; treat the authority as a teammate with veto power.

recall_advanced.q: The post-award stay rule, precisely.
recall_advanced.a: Stay if filed within 10 days of award or 5 days of the required debrief, whichever is later.

recall_advanced.q: Three venues and one distinguishing feature each.
recall_advanced.a: Agency — fastest/self-correcting; GAO — 100-day, automatic stay; COFC — binding, injunction instead of stay.

recall_advanced.q: Who authorizes an override, and on what two bases?
recall_advanced.a: HCA, written: urgent & compelling circumstances, or best interests of the United States.

recall_advanced.q: Task-order protest thresholds.
recall_advanced.a: $35M DoD / $10M civilian, or scope/period/ceiling growth at any value.

recall_advanced.q: Protest filed on day 9 after award, but the debrief was never requested. Stay?
recall_advanced.a: Day 9 is inside the 10-day award window — stay applies. The 5-day debrief branch only substitutes when a required debrief was requested and given later.

recall_advanced.q: GAO recommendations are 'advisory' — so ignore one?
recall_advanced.a: Legally advisory, practically followed — non-compliance is reported to Congress and torches agency credibility. Treat a sustain as a to-do list with a deadline.

recall_advanced.q: How do you protest-proof a source selection?
recall_advanced.a: You don't — you record-proof it: criteria stated and followed, evaluations contemporaneous and even-handed, meaningful discussions, an SSDD with real comparative reasoning, and a debrief that answers questions instead of provoking them.

recall_advanced.q: Four differences between an REA and a claim.
recall_advanced.a: Interest (claim only) · decision deadlines (claim) · prep costs (allowable REA / unallowable claim) · formality-certification.

recall_advanced.q: Claim certification threshold and the accrual limit.
recall_advanced.a: $100K; 6 years from accrual.

recall_advanced.q: What is a deemed denial, and what does it start?
recall_advanced.a: CO silence past the decision deadline operates as denial — the appeal clock starts.

recall_advanced.q: The two appeal routes and their clocks.
recall_advanced.a: Board of Contract Appeals, 90 days; COFC, 12 months.

recall_advanced.q: The contractor titled it 'REA' but demands a sum certain, certified, 'decision requested.'
recall_advanced.a: Substance over label — that's functionally a claim, and the CDA machinery (interest, deadlines) may already be running. Classify with Legal, fast.

recall_advanced.q: Why would a contractor choose the REA lane at all?
recall_advanced.a: Relationship preservation, allowable prep costs, speed, and settlement flexibility — the claim lane is leverage, but it burns goodwill and time.

recall_advanced.q: What must a differing-site-conditions recovery show first?
recall_advanced.a: Notice — the clause requires prompt written notice before conditions are disturbed, so the Government can investigate. No notice, weakened recovery.

recall_advanced.q: T4C settlement contents — and the profit rule.
recall_advanced.a: Costs incurred + reasonable profit on work performed + settlement expenses; no anticipatory profit.

recall_advanced.q: The T4D runway, in order.
recall_advanced.a: Cure notice → show cause → excusability analysis → T4D notice as final decision.

recall_advanced.q: Three classic excusable causes.
recall_advanced.a: Acts of God · sovereign/Government acts · fires/epidemics/similar events beyond control without fault.

recall_advanced.q: What happens to a T4D later found wrongful?
recall_advanced.a: Converts to a T4C — settlement owed instead of costs recovered.

recall_advanced.q: What does the contractor get in a T4C settlement?
recall_advanced.a: Costs incurred on the terminated work, reasonable profit on what was done, and settlement expenses — not the profit they hoped to earn on work never performed.

recall_advanced.q: You defaulted them; the board later finds the failure excusable. Now?
recall_advanced.a: The T4D converts to a T4C — with the Government paying settlement instead of collecting reprocurement costs. That's why the excusability record precedes the notice.

recall_advanced.q: When would you skip the cure notice?
recall_advanced.a: A pure failure to deliver on time — the schedule was the cure period. But when facts are mixed, send it; a needless cure notice costs ten days, a missing one can cost the termination.

recall_advanced.q: What makes BAA evaluation lawful competition?
recall_advanced.a: Public announcement + stated criteria + independent scientific merit review — selection against the standard, not between offerors.

recall_advanced.q: The three SBIR phases and Phase III's special property.
recall_advanced.a: I feasibility · II prototype · III production — no cap, sole-source eligible off competed early phases, SBIR rights persist.

recall_advanced.q: Two honest reasons to choose an OT — and one dishonest one.
recall_advanced.a: Honest: nontraditional participation; terms flexibility a prototype genuinely needs. Dishonest: "skipping the rules.".

recall_advanced.q: How is funding one BAA proposal 'competition' without comparing proposals?
recall_advanced.a: The BAA is a recognized competitive procedure: broad public announcement, stated criteria, independent merit review. The market competed by proposing; selection is merit against the standard, not against each other.

recall_advanced.q: Phase III SBIR sole source — really no J&A?
recall_advanced.a: The statutory program carries it when the work derives from competed Phase I/II — that's the authorized-by- statute lane. Document the derivation.

recall_advanced.q: When would you steer away from an OT?
recall_advanced.a: Traditional performers, well-understood requirements, or when the flexibilities aren't actually needed — OTs trade a mature protections framework for agility; spend that trade only when it buys something.

recall_advanced.q: The two Miller-Act-style bonds and whom each protects.
recall_advanced.a: Performance bond — the Government's work; payment bond — subs/suppliers who can't lien Government property.

recall_advanced.q: The differing-site-conditions notice rule and its reason.
recall_advanced.a: Written notice before disturbing the condition, so the Government can investigate.

recall_advanced.q: The personal-services test in one sentence.
recall_advanced.a: Continuous Government supervision of contractor employees creates an employer-employee relationship — unlawful absent specific authority.

recall_advanced.q: PBA's required elements.
recall_advanced.a: PWS (or SOO) · measurable standards · QASP · incentives where appropriate.

recall_advanced.q: Why can't you pick the A&E firm on price like everything else?
recall_advanced.a: Statutory design: qualifications-based selection, then negotiate a fair price with the most qualified — design quality drives lifecycle cost far more than design fee does.

recall_advanced.q: What's the difference between a PWS and a SOO?
recall_advanced.a: PWS: the Government defines outcomes and standards. SOO: the Government states objectives and offerors propose their own PWS — competition on approach, with the winning PWS becoming the yardstick.

recall_advanced.q: The COR is assigning daily tasks to contractor staff 'for efficiency.'
recall_advanced.a: That's the personal-services drift in action — direction flows to the contractor's manager against PWS outcomes. Fix the practice, retrain the COR, and check whether the PWS invites it.

scenarios.scenario: Eight months before a satellite-imagery software sustainment need begins, the PM tells you she's unhappy with the incumbent developer and "wants competition this time — put out an RFP next month." The system was built on the incumbent's commercial platform; the development contract delivered binaries and user manuals; the Government "probably has rights to something, nobody's checked." Two integrators have expressed informal interest, "assuming they can get the code."

facts.why: Desire isn't feasibility. An RFP before the rights-and-deliverables inventory is a solicitation you may have to cancel — strategy first, paper second.
The competition's real constraint: without source, build environments, and interface data, "assuming they can get the code" is doing tectonic work. What we hold decides what we can compete.
The platform rides its commercial license — a competitor needs lawful access. That's a licensing workstream inside the strategy, not a footnote.
Real market signal — formalize it with a sources-sought shaped around what the Government can actually furnish, and let their responses size the feasible competition.

scenarios.board_answer: Eight months is enough if we spend it right: first the data-rights and deliverables inventory — what we hold decides what we can compete; then a sources-sought built on what we can actually furnish; then the strategy call. If the inventory says competition isn't feasible yet, the honest plan may be a shorter incumbent bridge while we buy the deliverables that make next cycle competitive — and that gets written down as the strategy.

scenarios.scenario: During a staff visit you learn the fuels flight has been getting weekly analytics reports from a small software vendor since January. The squadron commander "approved it on a trial basis" after a vendor demo; the vendor now wants a PO for $95K covering the trial "as agreed." The commander points out he's a colonel with command authority, the unit genuinely uses the reports, and "there's end-of-year money to cover it." He asks you to just issue the purchase order this week.

facts.why: Rank and command authority are not contracting authority. Only a warranted CO binds the Government — this is apparent authority, which binds nothing.

facts.fact: The unit genuinely uses the reports
facts.why: Government benefit is real — that's one ratification element satisfied, and it's why ratification (not refusal) is the likely path.
The test is funds available when the commitment was made (January) and now — and the right color/year of money for what was actually received. "There's money lying around" isn't the test.
A PO now would paper over the violation. The path is a ratification package at the right level ($95K ≤ SAT → COCO), with the commander's signed statement in it.

scenarios.board_answer: That's an unauthorized commitment — command authority isn't contracting authority. I'd stop further performance, investigate, and build the RFO 1.405 ratification package: benefit's there, so it turns on fund availability in January and a fair-and-reasonable price; at $95K my COCO can ratify. And then I'd train that unit, because prevention is the real fix.

scenarios.scenario: Your SSEB chair calls: a technical evaluator just accepted a job with one of the three offerors — starting next month. The evaluator "hasn't told the team anything," has already recused himself from this week's consensus meetings, and says his new employer "only knows the program exists, nothing else." The PM wants to press on: "he recused himself, we're good — we can't slip the award for HR paperwork."

facts.fact: Evaluator accepting employment with an offeror
facts.why: Employment contacts between an offeror and a Government official with access to protected information are the PIA's second front. Self-recusal isn't self-clearing — this goes to Legal now, with a facts review of everything he touched and when the employment contact began.
His assurance isn't the standard. The question is what he had access to while employment discussions were live — that's established by record review, not by promise.
Recusal was right — but timing governs. Recusal after discussions began doesn't cure access that already happened.
Schedule pressure never outranks integrity of the selection. An award made on a tainted record invites protest and worse.

scenarios.board_answer: Recusal was step one, not the answer. I'd get Legal in immediately, establish when the employment contact started and what protected information he accessed after that, document it, and make the written determination whether the selection is compromised — and if it reached the offeror, that's the HCA's decision on how the procurement proceeds.

scenarios.scenario: Source selection for a logistics IT modernization is two weeks from FPRs. An offeror's capture manager, at an industry event, mentions to your COCO that a rival offeror "has our staffing rates — their teaming partner processes our subcontract invoices." The rival's proposal did come in with suspiciously well-aimed pricing. The SSEB chair suggests quietly normalizing the evaluated rates "so no one's advantaged," and notes that pausing now "looks bad for the program."

facts.fact: Teaming partner processes the competitor's invoices
facts.why: Classic unequal access to non-public information — a structural pipeline to a competitor's cost data. No intent needed; the imbalance is the conflict.
Evaluators can't launder an OCI through the evaluation. The conflict is investigated and resolved on the record, not adjusted away.
An award over an unresolved, documented OCI allegation looks worse — that's a sustained protest with the remedy chosen by someone else.
Suggestive but not proof. It justifies the inquiry; the determination rests on what access actually existed.

scenarios.board_answer: That allegation is unequal access — I'd get Legal in, establish the facts of what data actually flowed, and make a written determination. If access is real, I need avoidance, neutralization, or an enforceable mitigation before this selection proceeds — and note that handling an OCI during source selection isn't 'discussions,' so I can work it without opening exchanges.

scenarios.scenario: Award week on a grounds-maintenance IDIQ set-aside. Your apparent awardee — a small business — was terminated for default by another base fourteen months ago; their proposal explains new ownership and a rebuilt crew. The PM forwards a rumor from the old contract's COR that "these guys always bail mid-summer." Your specialist notes they're clean in SAM. The customer wants award Friday because the mowing season "won't wait for paperwork."

facts.why: A recent default squarely engages the performance-record standard. It's not automatically disqualifying — but it must be weighed on the record against the new-ownership facts.
Exactly the kind of countervailing fact the determination exists to evaluate. Verify it — org charts, key personnel, financing — don't just quote the proposal.
Hearsay isn't a finding. Chase it to documented performance history (CPARS, the T4D record) or drop it.
Necessary, not sufficient — exclusions and responsibility are different gates.
If the facts add to non-responsible, the SBA referral happens regardless of the mowing season — and the CoC may still direct award.

scenarios.board_answer: I'd make the determination on documented facts — the default record versus verified evidence of new ownership and capacity. Clean SAM isn't the test, and rumors don't count. If I land on non-responsible, they're small, so it goes to SBA for the CoC decision — and Friday moves if it has to.

scenarios.scenario: A depot needs specialized corrosion-inspection services, estimated $4.5M over three years. The incumbent's contract ends in five months. The PM hands you last cycle's market research — dated 26 months ago — showing "only the incumbent responded," plus an email from the incumbent's BD lead helpfully listing why competitors "can't meet the certification requirements." Your specialist mentions two small firms recently won similar work at another command.

facts.why: Past the 18-month currency line — it can inform, but it can't carry a new strategy. Fresh research is step one.

facts.fact: Incumbent's list of why competitors can't perform
facts.why: Market intelligence authored by the party that benefits from no competition is not market research. Verify independently or discard.

facts.fact: Two small firms winning similar work elsewhere
facts.why: Live evidence of capability — chase it: scope comparability, certifications, capacity. It bears directly on the Rule of Two.
Tight but workable — and "no time to research" is how bad bridges get born. The timeline argues for starting now, not skipping it.

scenarios.board_answer: That research is stale and the most persuasive document in the file was written by the incumbent — I'd run a fresh sources-sought now, engage the two small firms directly, and let the results drive the set-aside and competition decisions. Five months is enough if we start today; if it slips, a short bridge with a real cause beats a sole source built on a competitor's brochure.

scenarios.scenario: A squadron wants 400 task chairs "identical to the ones facilities bought last year from a local dealer — we already have a quote." Your inventory manager mentions a warehouse annex holding surplus furniture from a recently consolidated unit. The dealer's quote is 8% below the GSA schedule price for a comparable chair, and the squadron notes AbilityOne "only makes the fabric panels, not the chairs."

facts.why: Agency inventory and excess sit at the top of the ladder — before anyone's quote matters, that annex gets checked and the result documented.
Attractive, but the ladder isn't priced-ordered — it's priority-ordered. The quote matters only when the buy legitimately reaches the commercial rung (and then it's useful pricing evidence).
Fine — check the procurement list for what's actually covered and document the non-fit. That's the rung working as designed.

scenarios.board_answer: Ladder first: inventory and that annex, then UNICOR and AbilityOne against the procurement list, then schedules — and only then the dealer, whose quote becomes price-comparison data, not a shortcut. The file shows each rung and why we moved past it.

scenarios.scenario: A prime's $22M avionics upgrade proposal includes an $8M subsystem the prime bought "commercially" from its own subsidiary. Support: a one-page assertion citing "regular commercial sales," a catalog page with no prices, and a note that "per Part 12, no cost data is required." The subsidiary has sold the subsystem to exactly two customers — both foreign militaries — and your engineer says the Government's configuration adds a hardened chassis and MIL-STD wiring.

facts.why: "Sold to the general public" is the definition's spine — military-only sales history undercuts the assertion at its root. This is the fact to chase first.
Modifications get tested against form/fit/function. Militarization of this scale strains "minor."
A catalog proves a brochure exists. Commerciality pricing runs on actual sales at market prices — demand the sales data.

facts.fact: Prime bought from its own subsidiary
facts.why: An affiliated "commercial sale" deserves double scrutiny — the arms-length pricing discipline isn't there.
Backwards — the exception applies only after the determination holds. Assertion isn't determination.

scenarios.board_answer: The Government makes the commerciality call, not the proposal. On these facts — military-only sales, an affiliated seller, and militarizing mods — I'd likely find it non-commercial; and even if some element qualifies, I still require data sufficient to price it, certified or otherwise. The one-page assertion gets returned with a data demand attached.

scenarios.scenario: Friday, end of September. The CE squadron brings you four "urgent" buys: $14,800 of hand tools (GPC-ready, they say), another $14,600 of the same catalog's power tools, a $95K generator "only Vendor Z sells with the right output curve," and a request to "set up something so we stop doing paperwork every month" for HVAC filters. The GPC holder mentions the two tool buys "are from the same order the shop chief wrote up — we just split it to keep it simple."

facts.why: Same requirement, same catalog, same write-up: that's a ~$29K buy split to stay under the $15K MPT — the textbook violation. Recombine it into a purchase order, small business first.
Under-SAT sole source: document the single-source rationale (the output-curve requirement) and the price reasonableness — no J&A, but the reasoning goes on paper.
Repetitive, predictable, small: a BPA with established sources is the designed answer.
Fiscal-year pressure doesn't change any lane's rules — it's why the lanes exist. Fast is fine; splitting isn't.

scenarios.board_answer: The tool buys are one requirement — recombining them puts it in the purchase-order lane, reserved for small business. The generator is a documented under-SAT sole source. The filters become a BPA. And September doesn't amend Part 13.

scenarios.scenario: A $4.7M base supply-chain analytics requirement is ready to solicit. Your predecessor's file shows it was once an 8(a) award "years ago," then competed full-and-open last cycle after "SBA released it" (no release letter in the file). Research finds one very capable WOSB and one small firm whose capability statement is generic. The PM suggests a WOSB sole source "since she's clearly the best," and notes the incumbent large business "will protest anything we do anyway."

facts.why: If the requirement was never properly released from 8(a), its current posture is built on sand — confirm with SBA before any strategy is chosen. The paper matters.

facts.fact: One strong WOSB + one generic small firm
facts.why: The Rule of Two needs a reasonable expectation of two capable offerors — a generic capability statement gets probed, not presumed. The set-aside call turns on this.

facts.fact: "WOSB sole source, she's clearly the best"
facts.why: WOSB sole source has conditions and a ceiling — "best" isn't the test, and at $4.7M it must actually fit the program's sole-source lane ($5.5M other) and its conditions.
Protest fear is not a strategy input — a defensible record is the protest strategy.

scenarios.board_answer: First I'd confirm the 8(a) release with SBA — that decides whose requirement this even is. Then the Rule of Two on real capability evidence: if the second small firm doesn't hold up, a WOSB sole source is only available if the program's conditions and ceiling genuinely fit at $4.7M — otherwise compete it and let the record carry the protest.

scenarios.scenario: A PM bursts in: her ground-station modernization needs a new encryption module integrated "immediately — the wing commander is asking weekly." The incumbent integrator says it can start Monday. She's drafted a memo titled "Sole Source Justification — Urgent" for your signature, and adds that since the module rides on the incumbent's existing $60M integration contract, "we can probably just add it as a mod anyway." The module work is estimated at $2.8M. The existing contract's SOW covers "integration of communications and crypto subsystems as identified in the modernization baseline" — and this module is in the approved baseline.

facts.why: Pressure language pulling you toward a 6.103-2 urgency J&A. Command interest is not unusual and compelling urgency — no quantified harm, no mission stoppage.

facts.fact: The drafted "Sole Source Justification — Urgent" memo
facts.why: Someone else picked your authority before you analyzed the action. The board wants you to re-derive it.

facts.fact: SOW covers crypto subsystems in the approved baseline
facts.why: This is the fact that decides it: the work is arguably in scope of the existing contract. Run the scope analysis (Part 43 thinking: would offerors have anticipated it? cumulative impact?). If it's in scope, it's the M in SAMO — CICA doesn't apply and there is no J&A to write.
If scope analysis says it's new work, the action is over SAT → full and open unless a 6.103 exception holds, and at $2.8M your J&A approver would be the Competition Advocate.

scenarios.board_answer: Before I talk exceptions, I'd do a scope review with Legal — if this module is within the existing contract's scope, CICA doesn't govern and we execute a mod. If it's out of scope, competition is the default at $2.8M, and I'd need market research to support any 6.103-1 justification — command interest alone won't carry a 6.103-2 urgency.

scenarios.scenario: Tradeoff selection, $45M, discussions closed, FPRs in. Offeror A: slightly lower rated, price well below the Government's probable cost. Offeror B: modestly better ratings, much higher price. The SSEB chair worries B "will protest if they lose." Then you learn the SSA — without you — called Offeror A, told them their price "is way out of line with our probable cost," flagged conflicts between their EN responses and their FPR, and "gave them three ways to fix it."

facts.why: That call was discussions — after FPRs, with one offeror, inviting revision. Unequal exchanges with a single offeror after close is about as serious as Part 15 problems get. Stop everything; Legal now.

facts.fact: "Three ways to fix it" — compounds it
facts.why: Coaching one offeror toward award is disparate treatment on the record — the remedy has to be structural, not cosmetic.
Legitimately handled through the evaluation itself (realism on cost-type; risk assessment otherwise) — it never justified an off-record call.
Protest fear caused this mess. The cure is a clean record, and now likely: document the breach, reopen discussions with all offerors in the range, fresh FPRs — done with Legal's hand on the wheel.

scenarios.board_answer: My concerns are unequal discussions after close and disclosure of our probable cost to one offeror. I'd halt award, document the exchange, and with Legal likely reopen discussions with every offeror in the range and take new FPRs — the only fix for unequal treatment is restored equal treatment, on the record.

topics: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
scenarios.scenario: July 2026. You're the PCO for a sole-source $14M FPIF production add-on to a fielded ground radar — a new contract action, proposal in hand. The prime's proposal includes a $6M subcontract for RF amplifier modules with a ground rule: "the subcontract is commercial — pricing detail cannot be provided." The PM notes the original radar contract "was competed three years ago, so pricing's already been scrubbed," and finance wants award before the fiscal year closes. The prime's cover letter offers "summary-level cost data in the interest of schedule."

facts.why: Post-cutover action over $10M, sole source, no exception on its face → certified cost or pricing data is required. "Summary-level in the interest of schedule" doesn't satisfy the statute.
Adequate price competition excepts the action that was competed. This action wasn't. The exception fails at the action level.

A commercial determination, if it holds, excepts the subcontract from certified data — it does not excuse the prime's obligation, and I still need data other than certified sufficient to find the subcontract price fair and reasonable. First question: does the commercial assertion actually survive scrutiny?
Schedule never waives the statute. If time is truly critical, the honest tools are a properly supported proposal now, or leadership accepting the risk path with eyes open — not thin data.

scenarios.board_answer: This is a $14M sole-source action after the June 2026 cutover, so certified cost or pricing data is required — prior competition excepted the old action, not this one. I'd evaluate the commercial assertion on the $6M sub; if it holds, the sub is excepted from certification but I still need enough data to find its price fair and reasonable. Then price analysis plus element-by-element cost analysis with a real technical eval, weighted guidelines for profit, PNM and certificate at agreement — and the fiscal calendar doesn't change any of it.

scenarios.scenario: A PM wants to award a $28M "FFP" contract for operating and continuously improving a legacy data-processing pipeline — the improvement work is "whatever the ops tempo surfaces, we can't predict it." The contractor proposed a 12% fee "to cover the unknowns," and offers to "convert to T&M whenever things get fuzzy." The contractor has never had a Government cost-type contract and its accounting system has never been reviewed.

facts.why: The improvement scope is genuinely unestimable — that half of the work can't carry FFP. Structure it: FFP the defined operations, and put the unpredictable work in a separately typed lane sized to its risk.
Padding fee to absorb risk is the FFP failure mode in miniature — price risk through structure (type, incentive, ceiling), not through fee.
T&M is a last resort with a D&F, ceiling, and exit plan — not a convenience valve. An open conversion promise is an invitation to never estimate anything.
Whatever cost-type or T&M lane emerges, the accounting-system gate comes first — that fact constrains the whole menu.

scenarios.board_answer: I'd split the requirement: FFP the well-defined operations, and for the unpredictable improvement work pick a type that matches its risk — which first means dealing with the accounting-system gate. Fee doesn't absorb risk, structure does; and T&M only enters with a D&F and an exit plan, not as a standing escape hatch.

scenarios.scenario: Calibration-services MA-IDIQ, two holders: a large business at $7.1M of its $7.5M ceiling, and an SDVOSB at $2.6M of its ceiling, both minimums satisfied, three ordering years left. A $260K Phase II repair requirement arrives; the customer wants it awarded to the large business "as a logical follow-on to their Phase I win." The SDVOSB was rated technically acceptable in the Phase I competition. The large business's BD lead has already emailed you a draft SOW "to save time."

facts.why: The "logical follow-on" would nearly exhaust the large holder's ceiling with three years left — steering an order into a nearly-full ceiling is bad vehicle management even before fairness enters.

facts.fact: SDVOSB rated acceptable in Phase I
facts.why: A capable second holder guts "only one capable" and weakens "logical follow-on" — fair opportunity (or an order-level set-aside) is available and defensible.
A holder writing the order's SOW is a biased-ground-rules OCI in miniature — decline it, write our own, and note the contact in the file.
A $260K order competition between two holders costs days, not months — the time argument doesn't survive arithmetic.

scenarios.board_answer: I'd compete it between the holders — the SDVOSB proved capability in Phase I, so no exception honestly fits; and steering it would nearly max the large holder's ceiling anyway. The vendor-drafted SOW goes unused, and if the customer insists, the exception needs a D&A I don't think survives review.

scenarios.scenario: A depot-support contract's option two is due; notice date in 21 days. The COR's file: two quality escapes, both closed with corrective action, CPARS "satisfactory." The contractor emails: they'll "need a 9% price adjustment to keep performing" because of wage pressure — "or we'd understand a no-cost mutual walk-away." The PM says funding for the option year arrives in the new fiscal year, three weeks after the notice date.

facts.why: An option exercises at its priced terms — a contractor conditioning performance on a raise is refusing the option and inviting a negotiation. Exercise unilaterally at the option price, or don't; there's no "exercise at +9%."
The performance gate: documented, considered, and here probably passable — flags with completed corrective action are a judgment call to make on the record.

facts.fact: Funding arrives after the notice date
facts.why: Availability-of-funds mechanics exist for exactly this seam — align the exercise with the funds clause rather than obligating money that isn't there (the fiscal-law follow-up is coming).
That's the contractor negotiating against your leverage. The Government's alternatives — exercise, extend short, or recompete — get evaluated on their merits, not on the emailed menu.

scenarios.board_answer: The option exercises at its price or not at all — the 9% ask is a refusal dressed as a condition. I'd run the gates: performance is documented and arguably passes; the funding seam is handled through availability-of-funds mechanics; and if the contractor truly won't perform at the option price, my paths are a short extension while I recompete — with the record showing exactly why.

scenarios.scenario: September 12th. A PM arrives with a signed MIPR for $1.9M of current-year O&M to a civilian agency's assisted-acquisition shop for a "12-month analytics support task" — award expected "by December, they're backed up." The PM says the funds "are good because we're sending them before September 30th," and there's no interagency agreement on file yet, "but they say their standard one covers everything."

facts.why: Sending expiring funds cross-agency doesn't extend their life — the bona fide need and obligation rules follow the money. A December award of FY-expiring O&M for services starting then is the parking scheme fiscal lawyers feast on.

facts.fact: "Good because we send them before Sep 30"
facts.why: Transfer isn't obligation. The clock runs until a qualifying obligation exists — moving money to another agency's account doesn't stop it.
Assisted acquisition requires the signed agreement — roles, terms, fees — before performance. "Their standard one covers everything" is not an agreement in our file.
The best-procurement-approach D&F is required — and "they're backed up until December" is evidence against this being the best approach.

scenarios.board_answer: Three problems: the funds question — expiring O&M doesn't gain life by traveling, so a December award likely fails bona fide need; the missing interagency agreement, which must be signed before we proceed; and the D&F, which has to honestly conclude a backed-up shop is our best approach. As written, I'd pull the MIPR back and either buy it ourselves or fix all three on the record.

scenarios.scenario: A CPFF software-integration contract runs 1 March to 28 February, funded with one year's O&M. On 12 February the contractor emails: costs will hit the ceiling in ten days because Government-furnished test rigs "were down for repairs half the year" — they request additional funds and note "we already told the COR about the rigs back in June." The PM wants to add this year's O&M "since the work slid into this year anyway."

facts.fact: Notice on 12 Feb for a ceiling 10 days out
facts.why: The limitation clause's 75% rhythm exists to prevent exactly this ambush. Late notice weakens any entitlement to more funds — establish what they knew and when.

facts.fact: Faulty GFP "reported to the COR in June"
facts.why: Defective GFP can ground a legitimate equitable adjustment — but telling the COR isn't notifying the CO, and an REA has its own lane. It doesn't convert into "send money" at the ceiling.

Which year's need is this? Work performed against last year's requirement is last year's bona fide need — funding it with this year's O&M is a Time violation. Expired funds from the proper year handle proper adjustments.

scenarios.board_answer: Three lanes, kept separate: the limitation-of-cost mechanics — late notice means no automatic entitlement; the GFP issue — a potential REA, evaluated on its own record; and the money — any adjustment funds from the appropriation that bore the need, likely the prior year's expired O&M, not this year's. And the contractor isn't obligated to perform past funding while we sort it.

scenarios.scenario: Sustainment planning for a mission-planning suite. The development contract file shows: module A built under the contract with program funds; module B adapted from the contractor's commercial product; module C built "on contractor IR&D, matured on contract" per the contractor. Deliverables: binaries only — source "available under a separate license, price on request." The assertion list from award names only module B. The PM proposes just emailing the whole package to two potential competitors "under NDA, to gauge interest."

facts.fact: Assertion list names only module B
facts.why: Restrictions live or die on the assertion list. Module C's "IR&D then matured on contract" story was never asserted — the Government's default position on C is strong, and the burden of proving otherwise is theirs.
Entirely Government-funded → unlimited rights. That's the clean core of any competition package.
The commercial base rides its customary license; the adaptation's rights follow the adaptation's funding. Component-level mapping, not system-level slogans.

Rights without deliverables are theoretical — if source and build artifacts weren't contract deliverables, competing sustainment may require buying them now. That's negotiating posture, budget, and schedule.
Not until the rights map is settled — releasing B or C prematurely hands the contractor a claim and the competition a taint.

scenarios.board_answer: Component by component: A is unlimited — Government-funded; B rides its commercial license with the adaptation's rights following its funding; and C was never asserted, so the contractor carries the burden if they want restrictions now. Before anything leaves the building, we settle that map — and the real constraint may be deliverables, since rights to source we never took delivery of don't compete a sustainment contract.

scenarios.scenario: An FFP contract delivers 120 vehicle-mounted jammers. Mod history: mod 3 added winterization kits (+$1.8M), mod 7 upgraded the power amplifier (+$4.2M), mod 11 added 20 units (+$6M). Now the PM wants mod 14: swap the jamming waveform suite for a new-generation library the vendor "already developed for another customer" (+$9.5M on an original $38M). "Each mod passed scope review individually," the file notes. The contractor hints that if mod 14 is competed instead, "the REA for disruption will be substantial."

facts.why: The test is cumulative against the original: $38M has become $59.5M+ with materially different capability. Individually-blessed mods don't immunize the sum.

Anticipation test: did the original competition's offerors bid expecting a next-gen capability swap? A vendor-proprietary library "from another customer" reads like new work other vendors could compete.
The tightest scope perimeter of all types — cumulative drift on FFP is judged harshly.
A disruption REA is priced and defended on its merits — it isn't a toll that buys out competition. Decisions made to avoid asserted REAs are decisions made for you.

scenarios.board_answer: Cumulatively this contract has grown more than half again and is about to change capability generations — judged against the original award, mod 14 is out-of-scope new work. It gets competed or carried on a real J&A; and the REA threat gets evaluated as an REA, not as leverage over my scope call.

scenarios.scenario: Mid-way through a CPFF sensor-integration effort, the contractor requests the Government furnish a $700K calibrated antenna range "like the one we let them use informally last year through the lab." The PM supports it: "we own one that's idle, it obviously saves the contract money." The lab chief mentions the informal arrangement ended after "some damage nobody ever sorted out."

facts.why: Savings speaks to best-interest — one of four. Burden, risk, and can't-otherwise-be-met still need answers on the record, from the requiring activity.
Property in contractor hands without contract coverage is the anti-pattern: no clause, no risk allocation, no accountability. Whatever happens next happens on contract.
Exhibit A for why informality fails — and a live input to the risk prong of the four-part test now.

scenarios.board_answer: Possibly yes — but properly: the PM documents all four justifications, the property goes on contract with the full clause set and marking, condition is baselined on delivery, and the old damage gets resolved first — because the last informal loan ended with damage nobody owned, which is exactly what the clause machinery exists to prevent.

scenarios.scenario: Day 210 after qualifying proposal on an urgent airfield-defense UCA. Obligations sit at 72% of NTE. Negotiations stalled over overhead rates; the contractor proposes "rolling the remaining scope into a follow-on UCA to keep momentum" and notes their proposed fee "shouldn't move — we took all the risk when we started without a price." The PM asks you to obligate "the last 28% now" so the funding doesn't expire.

facts.why: The 180-day clock is blown — this is now a reportable discipline failure. Definitization becomes the commanding priority, with any extension papered deliberately, not assumed.
Chaining UCAs to avoid negotiating is the exact abuse the limits exist for — a second UCA needs its own justification and senior approval, and "we couldn't close the first one" isn't it.

facts.fact: "Fee shouldn't move — we took all the risk"
facts.why: Backwards: with 72% obligated and actuals visible, the remaining cost risk is small — weighted guidelines should price the risk that remains, which argues fee down.
The 75% post-proposal cap says no — and obligating to rescue expiring funds is a Time problem stacked on a cap violation.
