scenarios.board_answer: We're past the definitization clock, so closing the negotiation is now the mission — no follow-on UCA, no obligations past the 75% cap, and no year-end money parked in an unpriced action. On fee, the actuals cut the other way: risk already burned down, and the weighted guidelines will show it.

scenarios.scenario: Negotiations on a $40M sole-source engine-overhaul action closed Thursday, $2.1M above the Government's objective. The PM wants award signed Monday "since we already had business clearance and the delta is only 5%." Your PNM draft explains the movement in two sentences: "positions converged after productive discussion; price determined fair and reasonable."

facts.why: Business clearance authorized opening negotiations — the result needs contract clearance. Two gates, two purposes; the first doesn't waive the second.
Movement from the objective is precisely what the PNM must explain — what changed, what facts emerged, why the final position is still fair and reasonable.
"Productive discussion" documents nothing. The PNM tells the negotiation's full story — that draft wouldn't survive the clearance meeting, and shouldn't.

scenarios.board_answer: Monday isn't the gate — contract clearance is. And before I take it there, the PNM has to actually explain the $2.1M: which cost elements moved, on what new facts, and why the result is still fair and reasonable. Business clearance opened the negotiation; it doesn't bless the deal.

scenarios.scenario: Award posted Monday for a base-communications recompete. The incumbent — who lost — requests a debrief Tuesday; you hold it the following Monday. Wednesday after the debrief, they file at GAO. The PM erupts: "That's day 9 after award for a required debrief held day 7 — they missed the 5-day window, right? Keep the new contractor working." Meanwhile the awardee offers to "keep going unpaid until it sorts out, as a good-faith gesture." Your Legal advisor is TDY until Friday.

facts.fact: Debrief held day 7, protest filed 2 days later
facts.why: The rule is 10 days from award or 5 from the required debrief — whichever is later. Two days post-debrief is timely; the stay attaches. The PM's arithmetic uses the wrong rule.
Performance is performance — paid or not, it violates the stay and taints the corrective-action space. Direct a stop in writing.
The stay isn't optional pending counsel's return — execute it now, reach whatever Legal coverage exists, and start the agency-report clock.

scenarios.board_answer: The protest is timely — five days from the required debrief controls, not ten from award — so I stop performance in writing today, awardee's goodwill notwithstanding. Then notifications, the agency report, and my statement of facts; and if the fielding schedule genuinely can't absorb 100 days, the HCA override gets considered on real urgency facts, not frustration.

scenarios.scenario: A services contractor submits a certified "claim" for $128K: $67K for extra reporting a departed Government analyst "required weekly for five months," $38K for a two-week facility-access lockout during an exercise, and $23K in "claim preparation and outside counsel fees." The COR "vaguely remembers the reports being briefed." The PM wants to "pay the access piece to make it go away and deny the rest verbally."

facts.why: Over $100K and certified — the CDA clock and interest are running. This gets a written CO final decision, not a verbal anything.
Constructive-change candidate: unauthorized direction, performed, arguably benefiting the Government. Entitlement analysis (who directed, was it beyond the PWS) before any quantum talk.
Government-caused suspension of access is classic delay entitlement — evaluate honestly; it may be the strongest element.
In the claim lane those costs are unallowable — the element fails as pleaded.

facts.fact: "Pay one piece, deny the rest verbally"
facts.why: Piecemeal cash without findings plus a verbal denial = interest still running and no appealable decision. One written final decision (or a negotiated global settlement with release) closes it.

scenarios.board_answer: It's a certified CDA claim, so interest is running and my output is a written final decision — or a settlement. Element by element: the lockout has real entitlement; the reports need a constructive-change analysis; the prep and counsel fees are unallowable in the claim lane. I'd negotiate a global resolution with a release if the facts support it, and decide formally what doesn't settle.

scenarios.scenario: A grounds-keeping contractor has missed QASP standards three months running. The COR's log is thorough. The PM demands "default them today — we have it all documented." The contract runs seven more months; the next-best source's rates are 22% higher; and the contractor's owner calls you personally: her equipment was destroyed in a hangar fire last month — "give me six weeks and a schedule adjustment and I'll be back on my feet." The fire is confirmed; the performance failures predate it by two months.

facts.fact: Three documented months of QASP failure
facts.why: Real grounds — but for a performance-failure default the runway is cure notice first, not "today." The documentation makes the cure notice strong; it doesn't replace it.
An excusable cause — for what it actually caused. It explains the last month, not the two before it. Slice the failure timeline in the analysis.
Reprocurement economics inform the business judgment (and excess-cost recovery math) — they don't decide excusability or entitlement to default.
Compassion isn't a contract action — but a cure notice with a realistic cure period is lawful, humane, and strategically sound all at once.

scenarios.board_answer: Cure notice today — the documented failures support it — with a cure period that acknowledges the fire's genuine impact on recent weeks. If performance doesn't recover, show cause, excusability analysis slicing pre-fire from post-fire failure, then the default decision with Legal. And the 22% figure waits for the reprocurement math, where it belongs.

scenarios.scenario: A lab team wants to "BAA" a requirement to build 40 ruggedized sensor pods "to the attached ICD, delivered within 14 months, evaluated on price and past performance." Separately, they want to hand a Phase III production contract to a firm whose Phase II was performed for another service — "SBIR is SBIR, right?" — and a colonel asks why you can't "just OT the whole thing since OTs skip the rules."

facts.fact: "BAA... to the attached ICD, price and past performance"
facts.why: That's a production buy with a spec and comparative factors — an RFP wearing a BAA nametag. BAAs buy research toward broadly stated objectives with merit review; this gets the Part 15 treatment it actually is.

facts.fact: Phase III off another service's Phase II
facts.why: Phase III derives from the work, not the agency — a competed Phase I/II anywhere in the program can carry Phase III. Verify the derivation and document it.

OTs exchange the FAR framework for negotiated terms — they don't suspend fiscal law, ethics, or the need for disciplined agreements; and their best use case (nontraditionals, prototypes) has to actually be present.

scenarios.board_answer: Three answers: the pod buy is a specification-driven production requirement — that's an RFP, not a BAA; the Phase III is likely fine because derivation follows the SBIR work, not the sponsoring service — we verify and paper it; and OTs don't skip rules, they trade frameworks — I'd use one where nontraditional participation genuinely needs it, not as a bypass.

scenarios.scenario: Week three of a $900K taxiway-repair contract: the contractor's excavator uncovers a buried debris field of old construction rubble not on any drawing, keeps digging "to stay on schedule," and a week later submits a $210K REA with photos. Meanwhile your facilities customer, thrilled with the same contractor's site crew, asks you to "add a clause so their foreman can take daily direction from our shop lead on small stuff — it'll save everyone emails."

facts.fact: Kept digging, notice a week later
facts.why: The differing-site-conditions clause demands notice before disturbance so the Government can verify. Late notice doesn't automatically kill recovery, but it damages it — and the photos don't substitute for the investigation we never got to do. Entitlement analysis with that lens.
A genuine Type-condition candidate — materially different from the indications. The merits may be real even while the notice failure discounts them.
That clause would write personal services into the contract — Government supervision of contractor employees. Direction goes to the contractor's foreman through the contract's terms, period.

scenarios.board_answer: Two answers: the REA gets an honest differing-site-conditions analysis — real merits, discounted by the notice failure that cost us our investigation; and no, we don't write a daily-direction clause — that's personal services. The shop lead's needs route through the PWS and the contractor's own supervisor.

scenarios.scenario: You inherit a services contract supporting a munitions test range: three-year base, two one-year options, option year one begins in 60 days. The COR emails you: performance has been "shaky since spring" — two missed surveillance reports and a near-miss safety writeup — but the PM "already told the contractor we're picking up the option, since re-competing would take a year." Meanwhile the contractor's program manager mentions on a call that they've been "doing a little extra environmental monitoring the range officer asked for back in March — we'll square up the cost later."

frameworks.why: Before exercising: price still fair and reasonable · funds available · option still meets the need and is the best method · contractor eligible in SAM · performance considered. Two missed reports and a safety writeup go straight into that determination — an option is a unilateral right, never an obligation.

Document the deficiencies now, engage the COR's surveillance records against the QASP, consider a letter of concern or cure path — the record you build is what makes any downstream decision (option, extension, termination) defensible.

The range officer had no authority to direct new work. The Government isn't bound — this is ratification territory: investigate, get the facts and a statement from whoever directed it, confirm funds were and are available, and route to the ratifying authority. Train the range officer — direction flows through the PCO only.
"Already told the contractor" binds nothing — only the PCO commits the Government. But it does create a communication problem you now manage deliberately.

scenarios.scenario: A lab complex needs custodial and preventive-maintenance support for the next five years, starting this October. FM says the requirement will be funded annually with O&M. The facility manager wants "one award covering all five years so we never re-do this," and suggests obligating the first two years now "since this year's money is healthy."

frameworks.why: Recurring custodial/PM support is severable — benefit delivered as performed. Annual O&M funds a period generally ≤12 months; two years of obligation from one year's O&M fails Time.

The five-year need is met by a base year plus four one-year options (services rail: base+options ≈ 5 years), each option exercised with the 17.204-1 gates and funded by its own year's money — continuity without violating the appropriation clock.
Healthy money isn't the test; bona fide need of the appropriation's period is.

scenarios.scenario: You solicited a $1.7M simulator-maintenance requirement full-and-open, 30-day response period, healthy industry-day attendance. One proposal arrives — from Meridian Support Group, priced 6% under the IGCE. The PM is delighted: "award it before they change their mind."

frameworks.framework: Competition — one offer after full and open
frameworks.why: The competition was full and open — one responsive offer doesn't undo that. Find out why the field passed (debrief the no-bids informally; the answers improve the next solicitation) and document it.

With one offer, "adequate price competition" needs care — price analysis against the IGCE, history, and market data carries the fair-and-reasonable determination. At $1.7M, no certified data (under threshold, and it's a competitive solicitation); other-than-certified data if the analysis needs it.
Speed is fine — skipping the price-reasonableness record isn't.

scenarios.scenario: A fixed-price contractor is 45 days late delivering deployable generator sets. Three weeks ago the COR emailed the contractor "keep at it — we need these units." The contractor now says the delay stems from a subcontractor's plant fire, "so it's excusable," and adds that since the Government "told us to keep working, you can't default us anyway." The PM wants them terminated today and the units bought elsewhere.

frameworks.framework: Terminations — default posture after late delivery
frameworks.why: Late delivery on FP supplies supports T4D without a cure notice — but the intervening "keep at it" message raises schedule waiver. Re-establish a firm delivery date in writing (show cause framing) before any default.
Fires can be excusable if beyond control and without fault at both prime and sub tiers — test whether the prime could have mitigated (second sources, schedule buffer). Slice entitlement by timeline.

frameworks.framework: Authority — the COR's email — bait, with teeth
frameworks.why: The COR can't modify the schedule — but the Government's conduct (through any agent) can still create waiver facts. Both things are true; fix the record.
If T4D holds, excess reprocurement costs are recoverable — buy the replacement reasonably and mitigate.

scenarios.scenario: A cyber vulnerability in runway-lighting controllers must be patched fleet-wide "within 60 days" per an operational order. One holder on your five-vendor infrastructure MA-IDIQ built the original controller firmware; the other four have never touched it. The program wants a $1.4M direct task order to the builder today, and asks whether you can "skip the paperwork given the threat."

frameworks.why: Two candidate exceptions: urgency (unacceptable delay in meeting the 60-day order) and only one capable (unique firmware knowledge). Pick the one the facts actually support — probably both braid together here — and write the D&A (over SAT), approved at the right tier ($1.4M → Competition Advocate), posted.
The exception is the paperwork lane — a D&A takes hours, not weeks, when the facts are real. Skipping it converts a defensible urgent award into a finding.
Confirm cyber-patch work is within the IDIQ's scope — an out-of-scope order is a new procurement no exception can save.

scenarios.scenario: During a source selection for base network services, your cost analyst mentions at a staff meeting — with two support contractors in the room — that "the incumbent's past-performance rating came back weaker than expected." Four days later, the incumbent's capture lead emails the PM asking to "discuss addressing any performance concerns before FPRs." The PM forwards it to you with: "harmless, they obviously heard nothing specific."

frameworks.why: A past-performance evaluation in an active selection is source selection information; saying it in front of support contractors is a disclosure. Legal now · facts · affidavits on what was heard and where it went · MFR from the analyst · written impact determination.
Evidence the information may have reached an offeror — that's the high-impact branch of the determination (and their "discuss before FPRs" ask is itself an improper exchange to decline in writing).

Impact is determined on the record, not presumed by the PM. If the selection is compromised, the HCA decides the path — and unequal-information problems can force reopened discussions or corrective action.

scenarios.scenario: A PM has $6M of this year's RDT&E and wants to start a four-year, ~$40M sensor-fusion prototype effort immediately. Her plan: award the whole effort now, fund it incrementally "as money shows up," and if RDT&E runs short in the out-years, "O&M can cover integration and test since that's kind of operations." She wants the strategy meeting tomorrow.

frameworks.framework: Purpose — the O&M plan fails now
frameworks.why: Development integration and test is development — RDT&E work can't ride O&M "later." Kill that branch in the strategy meeting, on the record.

frameworks.framework: Structure — incremental funding on a cost-type development
frameworks.why: A cost-type effort can be incrementally funded with Limitation of Funds discipline — but the award must match honest funding expectations, and unfunded out-years are program risk to surface, not paper over.
A prototype producing a single outcome leans non-severable — check whether discrete fundable phases (design → build → test) can structure the effort honestly instead.
Hope is not a funding profile — the strategy documents what's programmed, and the contract's ceiling and clauses reflect it.

scenarios.scenario: A $780K interior-renovation contractor opens a wall and finds friable asbestos wrap on piping — none of the specs or drawings mention it. He stops work, photographs everything, notifies you in writing the same day, and states he "cannot finish the job at this price and wants to be paid for work done and released." The customer asks if you can "just make the scope smaller so he finishes the safe rooms and we call it complete."

frameworks.why: Immediate written notice before further disturbance: textbook. The condition (latent, materially different from the documents) supports an equitable adjustment for the changed work — abatement, schedule, price.

A DSC entitles him to an adjustment, not to walk away — performance continues under the adjusted terms once directed. If the Government's need truly changed, we hold the T4C/partial-termination pen, not him.

frameworks.framework: "Shrink the scope, call it complete" — bait, partially
frameworks.why: Descoping is legitimate — as a deliberate partial termination for convenience or deductive change, priced and papered — not as an informal handshake that leaves asbestos in the walls and entitlements unresolved.

scenarios.scenario: A wing exercise ends with leadership directing that a contractor-run 'innovation cell' be stood up within 90 days. The PM has a vendor in mind ('they briefed us at the symposium'), no requirements document, and asks you to 'start the contract paperwork while we figure out the details.'
baits: The 90-day directive implies urgency that hasn't been tested
'Vendor in mind' before any requirement exists
key_moves: No paperwork starts before a requirement definition — push for the need, outcomes, and an IGCE
Symposium familiarity is not market research — run a real capability look
Directed timelines don't create a competition exception; plan backward from 90 days with the real process
follow_ups: What belongs in the requirements conversation?
When would urgency legitimately shortcut competition?

scenarios.scenario: A services contract's final option year ends in 10 months. The program office says the follow-on 'will just be the same thing again' and asks you to hold off on strategy work until the new PM arrives in the spring — roughly 5 months out.
baits: 'Same thing again' minimizes the strategy work needed
Waiting for the new PM feels reasonable but burns the runway
key_moves: Start now — fresh market research, set-aside look, and requirement scrub take months
A bridge caused by waiting for personnel is a planning failure, not an unforeseen cause
Document the timeline so the record shows deliberate planning
follow_ups: What makes a bridge justification valid?
What could have changed since last award that invalidates 'the same thing'?

scenarios.scenario: A deployed civil engineer emails a portable-generator vendor 'we accept your quote, ship ASAP' to beat a storm window. The units arrive and work perfectly. The vendor invoices $65K. The engineer says exigency justified it and points out the base commander verbally concurred at the time.
baits: Genuine urgency and a good outcome make it feel excusable
Commander concurrence sounds like authority
key_moves: Neither engineers nor commanders hold contracting authority — this is an unauthorized commitment regardless of outcome
Government benefited and price may be fair → ratification package: statement, fund availability at the time, Legal
$65K ≤ SAT → COCO-level ratification; then train the unit on the emergency-buy channels that DO exist
follow_ups: Which ratification element most often fails?
What lawful rapid-buy tools existed for the storm?

scenarios.scenario: Reviewing invoices, you find a contractor billing 15% over the award for 'verbal expansions approved by the site lead' across six months — small additions each time, all documented in the contractor's notes but never in a mod. The site lead says 'that's how we've always flexed the work.'
baits: 'How we've always done it' normalizes the violation
Small increments hide the cumulative problem
key_moves: Site leads don't direct work — stop the practice in writing immediately
Sort what happened: unauthorized new work (ratification lane) vs. Government-directed changes to existing work (constructive change/REA lane)
Fix the channel: all direction through the PCO, and brief both the site and the contractor
follow_ups: How do you distinguish ratification from constructive change here?
What does the cumulative 15% do to your scope analysis?

scenarios.scenario: During proposal evaluations, an SSEB member's spouse posts on LinkedIn congratulating her company — one of the offerors — on 'great momentum on the base network bid.' The evaluator swears he's never discussed the source selection at home and offers to keep evaluating 'since nothing actually leaked.'
baits: 'Nothing actually leaked' — unproven and not his call
The post may be innocent, making inaction feel safe
key_moves: Report to Legal now — the question is what protected information was accessible and whether any moved
The evaluator's continued participation is a decision for the PCO/SSA with Legal, not a self-assessment
Document the facts and the determination whichever way it lands
follow_ups: What's protected under 3.104?
When does an appearance problem become a disqualification problem?

scenarios.scenario: A week before award, an offeror's VP calls your COCO: 'We heard we're rated second on past performance — we'd like to submit supplemental references.' Nobody outside the team should know any ratings. The COCO wants to 'just decline the references and move on quietly.'
baits: Declining the references feels like it contains the problem
'Move on quietly' avoids schedule pain
key_moves: The call itself is evidence protected information leaked TO an offeror — the serious branch of PIA
Legal immediately; trace the leak; written impact determination — quiet handling creates the protest AND the scandal
Decline the references in writing as an improper exchange, but that's the smallest part of the response
follow_ups: Who decides whether the procurement proceeds?
What are the offeror's obligations when it receives protected info?

scenarios.scenario: Your engineering-support contractor is helping the program office draft test criteria for an upcoming production competition. You learn the contractor's parent company just acquired one of the likely production bidders. The contractor proposes a firewall memo: separate teams, separate buildings, no shared drives.
baits: The firewall sounds robust and proactive
The acquisition just happened — 'nothing improper occurred yet'
key_moves: Test criteria authorship for a competition your affiliate will enter = biased ground rules — the hardest OCI to mitigate
Firewalls address information flow, not ground rules already being shaped — likely remedy is removing the contractor from the criteria work or excluding the affiliate
PCO decides, Legal advises, before the solicitation moves
follow_ups: Why don't firewalls fix biased ground rules?
What would a valid path look like if the Government wants the affiliate to compete?

scenarios.scenario: On your A&AS multiple-award IDIQ, Holder A's analysts maintain the program's requirements database. A new task order competition opens to all five holders — and Holder A's proposal cites specific unfunded requirements from that database as 'anticipated growth' no other holder mentions.
baits: Holder A did nothing overtly wrong — they used what they knew
The insight makes their proposal genuinely better
key_moves: Unequal access to non-public information — no bad act required; the imbalance is the conflict
Options: neutralize (share the same data with all holders and allow revisions) or address Holder A's access in the evaluation, with Legal
Fix the structure: database-support roles need OCI clauses and data walls before the next competition
follow_ups: Can you cure this mid-competition? How?
What contract language prevents this on support task orders?

scenarios.scenario: Your apparent awardee on a $700K paving contract lists an office address that turns out to be a mailbox store, has no equipment in its own name ('we lease everything per job'), and its listed superintendent also appears full-time on another company's website. Price is excellent and references check out by phone.
baits: Good references and price pull toward award
Leasing equipment is legitimately common in construction
key_moves: Run the standards on facts: organization, equipment access, key personnel actually available — a pre-award survey fits here
Leasing is fine IF the lease commitments are real — ask for them
If it nets to non-responsible and they're small: SBA referral for the CoC decision, not a quiet pass-over
follow_ups: Which of the seven standards are in play?
What does a CoC do to your determination?

scenarios.scenario: A contractor you terminated for default eight months ago is the apparent low offeror on a new solicitation — bidding through a newly formed LLC with the same owners, same address, and a fresh CAGE code. Your evaluator says 'new entity, clean slate, we can't hold the past against them.'
baits: 'New entity' formalism
Fear that considering history is prejudice
key_moves: Responsibility looks through paper: same owners and operations means the performance and integrity record follows them
The T4D is exactly the kind of documented history the standards exist to weigh — considering it is the job, not prejudice
Document the affiliation facts; if small and heading to 'no,' SBA referral still applies
follow_ups: What distinguishes a legitimate fresh start from evasion?
What system checks reveal the connection?

scenarios.scenario: For a niche electronic-warfare training service, your sources-sought draws zero responses. The PM takes it as proof only the incumbent can perform and asks you to start the J&A. The notice ran 10 days over a holiday period, used the program's internal acronym in the title, and posted under a generic NAICS.
baits: Zero responses looks like market absence
The PM's conclusion matches what the program wants anyway
key_moves: Zero responses to a badly shaped notice proves nothing — fix the title, NAICS, period, and do direct outreach
A J&A built on defective research is protest bait — the market-research section is its spine
Document round two either way; absence must be demonstrated, not inferred
follow_ups: What makes a sources-sought effective?
How much research is enough for a $10M sole source?

scenarios.scenario: The program wants a custom-built environmental test chamber and has written a 40-page spec. Your research finds three commercial chamber makers whose catalog units meet every parameter except one vibration profile — which two vendors say they routinely add as a factory option.
baits: The 40-page spec presumes custom development
'Except one parameter' feels like disqualification
key_moves: Research exists to reshape requirements: a catalog unit plus a routine factory option is likely a commercial product with minor modification
Rewrite toward performance terms; a commercial determination unlocks Part 12 streamlining
Document the comparison analysis — it becomes the CID's core
follow_ups: What makes a modification 'minor'?
What does Part 12 change about this buy?

scenarios.scenario: A unit orders custodial supplies monthly from a commercial e-commerce site using the GPC because 'it's cheaper than the mandatory source and delivery is faster.' Annual spend across the unit: about $140K, in individual orders that never top $3K.
baits: Each swipe is legitimately under the MPT
Cheaper-and-faster feels like good stewardship
key_moves: Mandatory sources (AbilityOne procurement-list items especially) aren't price-optional — check what's actually covered
$140K of predictable annual demand is one requirement wearing 50 swipes — structure it (BPA/consolidated buy) through the source ladder
Fix the unit's process, not just this order
follow_ups: Walk the supplies priority ladder
When does GPC use become splitting?

scenarios.scenario: Your customer wants specific network switches 'exactly like GSA Advantage shows, from Vendor Q's schedule listing, $290K.' A quick eBuy check shows four other schedule holders carry the same OEM line, two with published prices 6-9% lower.
baits: 'GSA already negotiated the price' — schedule fair-and-reasonable ≠ order fair-and-reasonable
The customer's vendor preference
key_moves: On schedules, the ordering CO still determines the order price fair and reasonable — compare holders, seek discounts
Four holders with the same line = easy comparison; document the quotes and the basis
Vendor preference without a differentiator is steering
follow_ups: What does GSA's determination actually cover?
When can you limit consideration to one schedule holder?

scenarios.scenario: A vendor proposes its 'commercially available' logistics-analytics platform for $4.2M. Digging in: the platform has one prior sale — to a foreign navy — and the proposal's 'catalog' was created last month. The vendor stresses the underlying database engine is genuinely COTS with millions of users.
baits: The genuinely-COTS engine launders the whole platform
A 'catalog' document exists
key_moves: Commerciality is determined at the level of what you're buying — the platform, not its ingredients
One military sale + a fresh catalog ≠ sold to the general public; the assertion likely fails
Component-level analysis may still except real COTS pieces; the rest needs data to price
follow_ups: What evidence establishes 'of a type' sold commercially?
What data can you demand if it's non-commercial?

scenarios.scenario: A commercial-items contract for fleet telematics is going badly — units fail in cold weather. The PM asks you to 'send a cure notice and start the T4D like we did on the radar contract.' The contract was awarded under Part 12 with the standard commercial clause.
baits: The radar-contract playbook feels transferable
'Cure notice / T4D' vocabulary is muscle memory
key_moves: Part 49 machinery doesn't run commercial contracts — the commercial clause's termination-for-cause framework does
Rights and remedies come from the clause: notice, opportunity, cause standards — with Legal on the specifics
The performance record and re-procurement logic still matter; the procedure differs
follow_ups: How does termination-for-cause differ from T4D in effect?
What does the Government owe on a commercial convenience termination?

scenarios.scenario: An exercise planner needs 30 days of portable toilets, fencing, and light towers across three sites — about $120K total. A staff sergeant already collected one quote per item from 'the companies we used last year' and asks you to cut three POs today so setup can start Monday.
baits: Pre-collected single quotes feel like completed legwork
Monday deadline
key_moves: The band is small-business reserved — confirm the vendors' size or solicit competitors
One quote per item at $120K needs price-reasonableness support: add quotes or comparison evidence fast
SAP can absolutely hit Monday — done properly it's hours, not weeks
follow_ups: How many quotes is 'enough' under SAP?
Could a BPA serve the recurring exercise cycle?

scenarios.scenario: September 28th. A flight has $47K of expiring O&M and a wish list: two years of software licenses ($22K), a training course occurring in November ($9K), and 'stocking up' on toner and cables ($16K). 'Just get it obligated by Friday.'
baits: Everything is under the SAT so it feels easy
Use-or-lose framing
key_moves: Two years of licenses on one-year money fails Time — current-year period only
November training: bona fide need analysis (when does the need arise?) with FM
Reasonable stock replenishment is fine; hoarding isn't — document the consumption basis
follow_ups: When can a current-year obligation serve next-year performance?
What's the severability of a license term?

scenarios.scenario: Market research for a $3.1M cyber-hygiene assessment shows five interested firms: three small (one 8(a), one WOSB, one plain small) and two large incumbents from predecessor work. The customer worries small firms 'can't handle the clearances' — though all three hold facility clearances per DISS.
baits: The clearance worry is asserted, and disproven, in the same breath
Incumbent gravity
key_moves: Rule of Two is met on documented capability — set-aside required posture, and check the socioeconomic programs before the plain set-aside
The clearance objection died in DISS; record it as resolved
Wrong-direction pressure gets answered with the file, DD 2579 coordinated
follow_ups: Order of precedence among 8(a)/HUBZone/SDVOSB/WOSB and total set-asides?
What breaks a Rule-of-Two expectation legitimately?

scenarios.scenario: An 8(a) firm has performed your base's grounds maintenance for six years across two competed-in-8(a) awards. The follow-on estimate is $5.8M. The district SBA office is slow answering emails, and the PM suggests 'just doing it full-and-open this time — more competition is always better, right?'
baits: 'More competition is always better' sounds virtuous
SBA slowness invites unilateral action
key_moves: Once in 8(a), the requirement stays unless SBA releases it — full-and-open without release is a program violation, not extra competition
$5.8M exceeds the competitive-threshold family → competitive 8(a) is the likely lane
Chase the release question through channels, documented
follow_ups: When is release from 8(a) appropriate to request?
Competitive vs. sole-source 8(a) — what sets the line?

scenarios.scenario: A depot needs OEM-proprietary calibration of 12 test stands. The OEM quotes $480K. Your predecessor's file contains three identical annual J&As citing 'only one responsible source,' each noting 'the Government intends to develop organic capability' — which never happened.
baits: Three approved J&As feel like precedent
The OEM lock may be genuinely real
key_moves: Repetition weakens, not strengthens: each J&A promised barrier-removal actions that never occurred — this year's must address that honestly
Attack the barrier: data/licensing for organic or third-party calibration priced as a line of effort
If the lock is real this year, the J&A can still be truthful — about the failure too
follow_ups: What does 6.104-1 require about overcoming barriers?
Who approves at $480K?

scenarios.scenario: A lab wants to award a $2M 'study extension' to the university that just finished a basic-research grant, sole source, 'to preserve research continuity.' The work statement reads like applied development with deliverable prototypes. The lab argues grants don't need J&As so neither should this.
baits: Grant history blurs the instrument question
'Continuity' as an all-purpose justification
key_moves: Name the instrument first: prototype deliverables for Government benefit = acquisition (contract), not assistance — competition rules attach
Continuity can support a 6.103-1 case only with market research showing unique capability
If it's genuinely basic research, a BAA or assistance lane may fit — but the SOW says otherwise
follow_ups: Acquisition vs. assistance — the test?
Could a BAA have covered this from the start?

scenarios.scenario: Mid-evaluation on a trade-off selection, the SSEB discovers every offeror misread an ambiguous PWS paragraph the same way — pricing 24/7 coverage the Government never intended. The SSA wants to 'just evaluate what they offered and fix it with the winner after award.'
baits: Uniform misreading feels evaluable ('same playing field')
Fixing post-award avoids schedule slip
key_moves: A materially defective solicitation isn't cured by consistent confusion — amend, and give offerors a chance to revise
'Fix it with the winner' = negotiating scope after award: pricing shifts, protest exposure, scope questions
Amendment now costs weeks; the alternative costs the competition
follow_ups: When does an amendment require proposal revisions?
What if the ambiguity surfaced after award instead?

scenarios.scenario: After award, the losing offeror's debrief question list includes: their own weaknesses (fine), the winner's proposed staffing plan, the winner's price broken out by CLIN, and 'all evaluator notes mentioning our company.' The PM wants to 'give them everything so they feel heard and don't protest.'
baits: Generosity as protest-avoidance strategy
'Feeling heard' conflated with disclosure
key_moves: Debriefs disclose the requester's own evaluation, the evaluated award result and rationale — never the winner's proposal details or CLIN pricing
Over-disclosure creates the next problem (winner's proprietary data released)
A quality debrief is thorough about THEM — that's what actually prevents protests
follow_ups: What must a post-award debrief include?
What's releasable about the awardee?

scenarios.scenario: Negotiating a $16M sole-source sustainment mod (awarded July 2026), the contractor certifies its data. Three weeks after agreement on price — before the mod is signed — their sweep surfaces a vendor quote 22% below the one in the proposal for a major material item.
baits: 'We already agreed on price'
The sweep feels like good faith that shouldn't be punished
key_moves: Pre-award discovery: use the corrected data — adjust the price downward before signature
The certificate speaks as of the date of agreement; incorporating the correction protects both sides
Document the adjustment in the PNM; good-faith sweeps are exactly why the process works
follow_ups: Same facts discovered 6 months after award — what changes?
All five defective-pricing elements?

scenarios.scenario: A contractor offers to 'save everyone time' on a $14M sole-source development action: they'll accept FFP if the Government skips 'the whole certified data exercise,' arguing the fixed price transfers all risk so the data doesn't matter.
baits: Risk-transfer logic sounds economically clever
Everyone loves skipping the exercise
key_moves: Contract type is not a CLAWM exception — over threshold, sole source, non-commercial = certified data, period
An FFP priced without data analysis just locks in an unanalyzed number — risk transfer at an unknown premium
Separately evaluate whether FFP even fits development-grade uncertainty
follow_ups: Recite CLAWM
Why is unanalyzed FFP worse than analyzed cost-type here?

scenarios.scenario: A PM wants CPFF for a follow-on production lot of 200 proven units, 'because the contractor says material prices are volatile and won't hold a firm price.' Cost history from three prior FFP lots is extensive and stable except for two commodity metals.
baits: Contractor preference presented as necessity
Real-but-narrow volatility inflated into type-wide uncertainty
key_moves: Mature production with deep cost history is FP territory — the named risk is two commodities, not the effort
FFP with economic price adjustment scoped to those indices prices the actual risk
CPFF on stable production shifts all cost risk to the Government for no reason — and check the E.O. 14402 justification implications of going non-FFP
follow_ups: How does an EPA clause get structured?
When would production legitimately be cost-type?

scenarios.scenario: On an FPIF negotiation — target cost $20M, target profit $1.6M, ceiling 125%, share 80/20 — the contractor's final position quietly moves the ceiling to 135% 'to reflect supply-chain reality' while leaving everything else unchanged. The PM thinks that's harmless 'since we only pay actuals plus profit anyway.'
baits: 'We only pay actuals' misunderstands FPIF
One parameter moving 'quietly' among four
key_moves: The ceiling is the Government's hard protection — raising it moves the PTA and extends Government exposure by $2M
Run the PTA math both ways and show the delta; price any real supply-chain risk explicitly instead
Every FPIF element is negotiated geometry; nothing moves 'quietly'
follow_ups: Compute PTA before and after
What happens to contractor behavior past PTA?

scenarios.scenario: On a 4-holder engineering IDIQ, the program shapes a new task order around a proprietary modeling tool that only Holder C owns — the requirement literally names the tool. Asked why, the PM says 'their engineer demoed it and it's exactly what we need.'
baits: Naming the tool feels like precision, not steering
The demo genuinely was impressive
key_moves: A requirement written around one holder's proprietary product is steering wearing a spec costume — restate to performance terms
If only the tool truly satisfies the need, that's an 'only one capable' exception argument — made honestly in a D&A, not smuggled in
Fair opportunity means the other three get a real shot at the actual need
follow_ups: What belongs in the D&A if the tool is genuinely unique?
How does this differ from a brand-name justification in open competition?

scenarios.scenario: A $9M task order for logistics software support is at month 30 of 36. The program wants to add data-migration work for a completely different system owned by another PEO — 'the vehicle's ceiling has room and the contractor is willing.'
baits: Ceiling room framed as authority
Contractor willingness framed as feasibility
key_moves: Ceiling is capacity, not scope — test the new work against the IDIQ's scope and this order's
Another PEO's unrelated system is a new requirement: fair opportunity on this vehicle (if in scope) or a new procurement (if not)
Out-of-scope orders are protestable at any dollar value as improper sole-source awards
follow_ups: Who protests an out-of-scope order and where?
What analysis documents an in-scope conclusion?

scenarios.scenario: Exercising option year 2 of a lab-services contract, you discover the option CLIN was never priced at award — the schedule says 'TBD, to be negotiated.' The COR has already emailed the contractor that 'the option is being picked up' and performance continues seamlessly in three weeks.
baits: Seamless continuity pressure
The COR's email creating apparent momentum
key_moves: An unpriced 'option' isn't an option — there's no unilateral right to exercise; it's a negotiation (and its competition posture needs Legal now)
The COR email binds nothing but complicates the negotiation — correct it in writing
Bridge honestly if needed while the real path (negotiate/compete) is worked
follow_ups: What made the option invalid at award — evaluation or pricing?
What are the Government's lawful continuity tools here?

scenarios.scenario: An option must be exercised by 15 September for a performance period starting 1 October. FM says the new fiscal year's funds obviously don't exist yet, and the PM concludes 'so we legally can't exercise until October — the contractor will just have to gap two weeks.'
baits: The fiscal logic sounds airtight
A two-week gap normalized as inevitable
key_moves: The availability-of-funds mechanism exists for exactly this: exercise subject to availability, obligation upon funds
Missing the 15 September date kills the unilateral right — that's the real risk in the room
Coordinate the clause mechanics with FM now; no gap required
follow_ups: What does the funds-availability clause actually promise the contractor?
What if funds never materialize?

scenarios.scenario: An outfit wants to send $3.2M to another agency's 'rapid-tech marketplace' office, which promises award in 30 days through 'pre-competed innovation vehicles.' The one-page flyer doesn't identify the underlying contracts, the fee is 6%, and the PM says 'everyone at the symposium uses them.'
baits: Speed and social proof
'Pre-competed' as a magic word
key_moves: Identify the actual vehicles and authority before a dollar moves — 'marketplace' is marketing, not analysis
Over SAT to a non-DoD shop → best-procurement-approach D&F: alternatives, fee scrutiny, servicing agency's track record
Assisted acquisition needs the signed interagency agreement; our fiscal rules travel with the money
follow_ups: What makes the 6% fee acceptable or not?
Direct vs. assisted here — which is this?

scenarios.scenario: Last September your office MIPRed $1.5M of O&M to a servicing agency for a training-support task. It's now July; their CO reports $410K will go unspent when the task ends next month, and their program office suggests 'rolling the remainder into a follow-on task so the funds don't go to waste.'
baits: 'Don't go to waste' — the eternal siren
The servicing agency's helpfulness
key_moves: Unobligated MIPR balances come home — they don't become the servicing agency's seed corn
The FY25 O&M is expiring; a new follow-on task is a new (current-year) need
Recover the funds, close the agreement cleanly, fund any follow-on properly
follow_ups: What happens to the recovered funds now?
Who tracks interagency balances — and how often should you?

scenarios.scenario: A small business on an FFP production contract asks for progress payments, then mid-year requests the rate be raised 'to the max allowed' and asks whether the Government can also pay for a materials stockpile it wants to pre-buy against future orders that aren't on contract yet.
baits: Small-business sympathy
'Max allowed' framed as an entitlement
key_moves: Progress payments follow the clause rates; customary financing is fine — but payments attach to THIS contract's performance
Financing a stockpile for hoped-for future orders isn't contract financing — it's an advance against nothing
If cash flow is the real issue, performance-based payments or delivery scheduling may honestly help
follow_ups: Order of preference for financing methods?
What protects the Government in progress payments (title, liquidation)?

scenarios.scenario: A contractor delivers the final technical data package for a missile-handling trailer — every drawing stamped with limited-rights legends, including drawings the Government watched them create under this fully Government-funded contract. 'Standard company template,' their data manager shrugs, offering to 'sort it out during sustainment.'
baits: 'Template' minimization
Deferral to sustainment (when leverage is gone)
key_moves: Government-funded development = unlimited rights; the legends are nonconforming markings — challenge/correct now, in writing
'Sort it later' means competing sustainment against markings you accepted silently
The assertion list from award is the yardstick — unasserted restrictions carry the contractor's burden
follow_ups: The marking-challenge sequence?
What if some drawings genuinely mixed in private-expense heritage?

scenarios.scenario: A small firm's SBIR Phase II produced a promising power-management module. Years later, your program wants the design data to second-source production. The firm asserts SBIR data rights; your engineer argues 'the protection must be expired by now,' and the PM suggests just reverse-engineering it from delivered units.
baits: 'Must be expired' — assumed, not verified
Reverse-engineering framed as a clean workaround
key_moves: SBIR protection runs long — verify the actual window from the contract and delivery dates before anyone acts
Reverse-engineering has its own legal limits and practical costs; it's a Legal conversation, not a shop decision
The durable fix is negotiating rights or a license priced against the second-source business case
follow_ups: What do SBIR rights protect during the period?
What happens to the rights when the window closes?

scenarios.scenario: A firm-fixed-price contract delivers training courseware in English. Partway through, the customer asks to add Spanish and Portuguese versions — roughly 40% more content-hours — and the contractor cheerfully offers a 'no-cost mod' in exchange for a 10-month period extension and relief from two quality metrics.
baits: 'No-cost' hides the real price (time + quality relief)
Contractor cheerfulness
key_moves: Nothing about this is no-cost — schedule and metric relief ARE consideration; price the exchange honestly
New-language versions at +40% effort: run the four-corner scope test; this may be out-of-scope new work
If out of scope: competition or a justified exception — a mod can't carry it
follow_ups: What counts as consideration in a mod?
How does the anticipation test apply to added languages?

scenarios.scenario: During a base network upgrade, the Government's fiber-conduit maps prove wrong in six buildings — the contractor reroutes on the fly at the COR's verbal 'keep moving, we'll square up.' Four months later a consolidated $340K REA arrives. The PM objects: 'they never got a mod authorizing any of that.'
baits: 'No mod = no entitlement' — exactly backwards here
The consolidated lump obscures per-building facts
key_moves: Government-caused changes (bad maps + directed continuation) are constructive changes — the missing mod is the Government's paperwork failure, not the contractor's entitlement bar
Evaluate entitlement building-by-building, then quantum with technical support
Settle bilaterally with a release; and fix the direction channel
follow_ups: REA vs. claim consequences if this stalls?
Who had authority to say 'keep moving' — and what does that change?

scenarios.scenario: Closing out a five-year R&D contract, the property report lists 212 Government-furnished items; the contractor can locate 168. Of the missing 44, they say 30 were 'consumed in testing years ago' (no records), 9 are 'probably at the subcontractor,' and 5 are simply unknown. They propose closing out now and 'reconciling later.'
baits: 'Consumed in testing' as an unverifiable catch-all
Closeout momentum
key_moves: No closeout with an open property reconciliation — the leverage ends at closeout
Loss/damage/destruction process per the clause: investigation, liability determination under the risk allocation, records
Subcontractor-held property is still the prime's accountability
follow_ups: Who adjudicates property loss — and on what standard?
What does the contractor's property-management-system status change?

scenarios.scenario: To help a struggling FFP contractor meet schedule, the PM wants to lend them a Government CNC machine 'for a few months, informally — putting it on contract takes too long and they only need it for one part run.'
baits: Informality justified by brevity
Helping-the-schedule urgency
key_moves: No informal property loans — on contract with the property clause set or not at all
Furnishing property to an FFP contractor shifts risk and may found an REA if it's late or faulty — price/paper the arrangement deliberately
The four-part GFP justification still applies, brief or not
follow_ups: What happens if the informal machine breaks mid-run?
How does GFP alter FFP's risk story?

scenarios.scenario: A UCA for aircraft battle-damage repair was issued at a $30M NTE. The qualifying proposal arrives at $41M with a letter explaining 'actual damage exceeded initial survey.' The contractor requests the NTE be raised to match 'so definitization can proceed on real numbers.'
baits: 'Real numbers' framing makes the raise sound like accuracy
Definitization urgency used as leverage
key_moves: The NTE is the Government's liability ceiling — it doesn't float up to meet proposals
Is the extra damage in-scope growth (negotiate within/adjust deliberately with approvals) or new work (new action, new approvals)?
Definitize what was ordered; obligations stay inside the caps meanwhile
follow_ups: What approvals would an NTE increase require?
How do the 50/75% caps apply during this fight?

scenarios.scenario: Definitizing a 9-month-old UCA, the contractor proposes forward rates for the remaining work but resists providing actual incurred costs for the months already performed — 'the certified proposal covers everything going forward, and actuals would just confuse the comparison.'
baits: 'Certified forward proposal' sounds complete
'Confuse the comparison' — the confusion is the point
key_moves: Work performed has actuals — they're exactly what definitization pricing must use for the performed portion
Certified data spans the action; incurred costs are cost or pricing data
Fee reflects the burned-down risk in weighted guidelines — actuals are how you see it
follow_ups: Why does fee typically drop at definitization?
What audit support fits here?

scenarios.scenario: Your negotiation team reaches a handshake deal Friday on a $60M sole-source action — inside the objective. The contractor's CEO emails Monday asking to 'paper it this week before our quarter closes.' Clearance is scheduled in twelve days. The PM asks if you can sign now and 'ratify through clearance after.'
baits: Deal inside the objective feels pre-blessed
CEO/quarter pressure
key_moves: No award before contract clearance — the review is the approval, not a receipt
'Ratify after' inverts the design: independent eyes before commitment
Ask the clearance shop to accelerate on merits; that's the lawful fast path
follow_ups: What does the clearance authority review in the PNM?
What if clearance directs a position change after your handshake?

scenarios.scenario: Day 40 of a GAO protest on your IT award, agency counsel concludes the evaluation record has a genuine defect — one factor was scored against an unstated standard. GAO's decision is 60 days away; the PM wants to 'ride it out since we might still win.'
baits: 'Might still win' gambling with a known defect
Sunk-cost momentum
key_moves: Voluntary corrective action on a real defect beats a sustain: faster, cheaper, and you control the remedy scope
Riding out a known defect risks paying protester's costs on top of losing
Define the correction precisely (re-evaluate the factor, revised SSDD) — not a panicked full redo
follow_ups: What corrective actions are available?
How does GAO treat corrective action taken mid-protest?

scenarios.scenario: A holder on your MA-IDIQ emails a formal-looking 'protest' of a $4M task order award (DoD), citing unfair evaluation. It's below the GAO order-protest threshold and doesn't allege scope growth. The contractor CCs your SCO and threatens 'escalation to GAO and the Court' within five days.
baits: Formal formatting and CC-intimidation
The five-day ultimatum
key_moves: Under $35M with no scope allegation: GAO lacks jurisdiction — the lane is the task-order ombudsman
Treat it seriously anyway: review the order file, respond through the ombudsman process
No stay attaches; performance continues while the complaint is worked
follow_ups: What DOES get an order to GAO?
What does the ombudsman actually do?

scenarios.scenario: A contractor's $85K REA for Government-caused test-range delays has sat in your predecessor's inbox for seven months unanswered. The contractor's new letter converts it to a certified claim 'for $85K plus interest from the original submission' and demands a final decision in 60 days.
baits: Interest 'from the original submission' — check the actual trigger
Seven months of silence feels indefensible (it is, but it's not entitlement)
key_moves: Interest runs from receipt of the certified CLAIM, not the earlier REA — correct the math while owning the delay
Under $100K certification isn't required, but as submitted the decision clock is real: decide or settle within the window
Evaluate entitlement on the delay facts now — the merits didn't age out
follow_ups: Deemed denial — when and what follows?
How does the 6-year accrual limit interact with the seven months?

scenarios.scenario: After a partial T4C removed one of three sites from a custodial contract, the contractor's settlement proposal includes: costs at the terminated site (fine), 'unabsorbed overhead' spread across the surviving sites, anticipated profit on the cancelled option years, and $12K in settlement-proposal preparation costs.
baits: The plausible-sounding mix of allowable and not
Option-year profit smuggled into a convenience settlement
key_moves: Costs incurred + reasonable profit on work PERFORMED + settlement expenses = the frame; prep costs are generally allowable here
Anticipated profit on unperformed work (cancelled options especially) is out
Unabsorbed overhead is a real doctrine with strict proof — DCAA support, Legal on the standard
follow_ups: Why are settlement prep costs treated differently than claim prep costs?
What proof supports unabsorbed overhead?

scenarios.scenario: A key-supplier bankruptcy leaves your avionics contractor unable to deliver for at least nine months. They propose novating 'the whole contract' to a competitor who bought the supplier's assets — or, alternatively, ask the Government to T4C them 'so nobody's record gets hurt.' Units are needed in six months.
baits: T4C offered as a courtesy to their CPARS
Novation floated casually
key_moves: Bankruptcy upstream may be excusable delay — analyze before any termination posture
T4C isn't a record-laundering service; the decision follows the Government's interest, honestly recorded
Novation runs its own legal process (successor-in-interest, through Legal); meanwhile mission needs may drive reprocurement of the six-month quantity
follow_ups: Excusable vs. not for subcontractor failure?
What does a T4D require if delay proves non-excusable?

scenarios.scenario: Two months into a $2M roofing contract, the contractor's crews stop showing up; calls go unanswered for three weeks; the bonding company writes that the firm 'has ceased operations.' The PM asks whether you still have to send a cure notice to an empty office before defaulting.
baits: Process formalism ('must cure-notice a ghost?')
Ignoring the surety's role
key_moves: Ceased operations = anticipatory failure; document the abandonment record (attempts, surety letter) with Legal — the notice posture follows the facts
The performance bond is now the story: demand on the surety to complete or fund completion
Move fast; weather and schedule are running against an unmanned roof
follow_ups: What does the surety owe under the performance bond?
How do excess reprocurement costs work with a surety in play?

scenarios.scenario: An open BAA topic on autonomous logistics draws a white paper from a nontraditional startup — genuinely novel approach, weak cost volume, and a note that they 'won't sign anything giving the Government our IP.' The lab wants them badly and asks whether an OT fixes everything.
baits: 'OT fixes everything' — flexibility ≠ magic
Enthusiasm outrunning the rights conversation
key_moves: An OT can tailor IP terms — but the Government still needs SOMETHING durable: define minimum-essential rights against the transition plan
Weak cost volume gets fixed in negotiation regardless of instrument
Write the follow-on production pathway into the prototype OT now if you ever want it
follow_ups: What makes a performer 'nontraditional'?
What rights floor would you hold for a transition-bound prototype?

scenarios.scenario: A program office wants to award a Phase III SBIR production contract to a firm — but the firm was acquired last year by a large defense prime, and a competitor argues Phase III 'is a small business program, so they're ineligible now.'
baits: 'Small business program' intuition misapplied to Phase III
Competitor advocacy shaping the analysis
key_moves: Phase III has no size requirement and no dollar cap — eligibility follows derivation from the competed SBIR work, which survives acquisition
Verify the derivation chain and document it; the sole-source basis is the statute
SBIR data rights also survived the acquisition — relevant to everyone's expectations
follow_ups: What documents the derivation?
What happens to SBIR rights post-acquisition?

scenarios.scenario: A design-bid-build project for a maintenance hangar comes in: IGCE $8.4M. The draft solicitation announces 'estimated value $8.4M' verbatim, requires only a payment bond 'to save the contractor money,' and sets liquidated damages at $25K/day because 'that will motivate them.'
baits: Transparency instinct (publishing the estimate)
'Motivational' LDs
key_moves: Disclose the magnitude RANGE, never the estimate — protects the Government's negotiating position
Over the bonding threshold both performance AND payment bonds are required
LDs must be a genuine pre-estimate of daily harm — punitive rates are unenforceable
follow_ups: How is an LD rate derived defensibly?
Who is the payment bond actually for?

scenarios.scenario: Six months into a base operations support contract, the contractor's site manager quits. Rather than wait for a replacement, the squadron 'temporarily' assigns tasking through the Government flight chief — daily standups, direct assignments, leave approvals for contractor staff. Everyone agrees it's working great.
baits: Temporary-and-working normalizes the arrangement
Leave approvals buried in the list (the loudest red flag)
key_moves: Government supervision of contractor employees — down to leave approval — is personal services without authority; stop it now
The contract requires the contractor to manage its people: demand the replacement manager under the key-personnel terms
Document the interim fix that routes direction through the contractor's structure
follow_ups: What's the legal test for personal services?
What does the key-personnel clause let you demand?

scenarios.scenario: An audit flags that a unit paid a contractor twice for the same invoice eight months ago — $38K. The contractor never mentioned it. The PM suggests 'just deducting it from next month's invoice quietly' to avoid the paperwork of a formal demand.
baits: Quiet netting feels efficient
Eight months of contractor silence goes unremarked
key_moves: Overpayments are Government debts with a process: written demand, interest rules, FM coordination — not informal netting
The contractor's duty to report duplicate payments matters; note it in the record
Fix the payment-review breakdown that let it happen
follow_ups: When can you offset against invoices — and how formally?
What does the contractor's silence do to the relationship record?

scenarios.scenario: On a competitive cost-type source selection, one offeror's proposed labor rates run 30% below the DCMA-recognized rates for their own facility. Their technical volume is strong. An evaluator suggests scoring them down on technical 'to reflect the pricing games.'
baits: Punishing price problems in the technical score
'Games' assumed rather than analyzed
key_moves: The lane for low cost-type pricing is cost realism: adjust to a most-probable-cost for evaluation — the proposal competes at what it will really cost
Technical scores reflect technical merit; cross-lane punishment is protest fuel
Document the realism adjustments and their basis (DCMA rates)
follow_ups: Probable cost vs. proposed cost in the SSDD?
When does realism apply on fixed-price competitions?
